episodes.title: Killing of George Wallace (1869)
episodes.lead: The killing of George Wallace was the shooting of a young man by a squad of Arkansas state militia near Mound City, across the river from Memphis, on a Saturday in January 1869. Wallace fled on meeting the squad while carrying provisions to his mother and was pursued and killed instantly. The Memphis Appeal reported it as a murder by "Clayton's bandits" and reprinted the item in August 1888 as part of a record of "Despotic Republican Rule" in Arkansas.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Anthony Cantieny
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Anthony Cantieny took place at the Minneapolis jail around March 1885, during his trial for killing a police officer, when talk of lynching led the mayor to order out the military. Nobody was hurt, and Cantieny was convicted of manslaughter. It is known only from a St. Paul Daily Globe column of November 1888, which gave two versions of the threat.

episodes.title: Bald Knobber plot to lynch Almus Harrington
episodes.lead: The Bald Knobber plot to lynch Almus Harrington was a plan by the Bald Knobbers of Christian County, Missouri, to hang Col. Almus Harrington, an Ozark attorney, in September 1886. A force of 142 men led by the Knobber chief Dave Walker set out toward Ozark to carry out the resolution but abandoned the attack, and Harrington was unharmed. The plot became public in April 1888, when Harrington, then associate counsel for the State in the Bald Knobber cases, described it to a Globe-Democrat correspondent.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Alexander Goldensen
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Alexander Goldensen was a mob attack on a San Francisco jail in November 1886, in which a crowd tried to seize and lynch a young man held for shooting a 14-year-old schoolgirl, Mamie Kelly. The police drove the mob off, and reports of his execution counted two such attempts, both stopped by police. Goldensen was tried, convicted and hanged legally on September 14, 1888, an execution that the wire report said had excited more interest on the Pacific coast than any since the days of the vigilance committee.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of William Patterson and Albert Turner
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of William Patterson and Albert Turner was the siege of the Jefferson County jail in Louisville, Kentucky, by a mob intent on lynching the two Black prisoners, who were accused of fatally beating a domestic servant named Jennie Bowman. According to the wire account, the State militia guarded the jail for three days until the crowd dispersed, and both men were later hanged by law. The siege is known only from background paragraphs in reports of Patterson's execution on June 22, 1888, which in most versions date it to April 27, 1887; a Louisville dispatch that June also described a plot by a few citizens to lynch Patterson if he were pardoned.

episodes.title: Murder of John Aikens
episodes.lead: The murder of John Aikens was the killing of a 28-year-old Black farmer in Calvin township, Cass county, Michigan, who disappeared on the night of December 23, 1887, and whose body was recovered from a lake in early May 1888. Two young men, Lewis Wilson and Gus Harris, were jailed after Wilson confessed to a part in sinking the body. The confession drew wire coverage from Indiana to Washington, and one dispatch reported that "lynching feeling" against the accused ran high.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Washington
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of William Washington followed the killing of Mrs. Mary Miller, the young wife of farmer John Miller, near Ellinger, Texas, in late December 1887, for which Washington, a Black former servant of the family, was arrested. Wire dispatches of December 31 and January 1 predicted that he would be lynched within hours, and one reported proposals that he be tortured to death. No lynching was reported; in October 1888 papers reported that a William Washington, convicted of the rape and murder of a white woman near Columbus, Texas, was hanged there before a crowd of 2,000 to 3,000.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Fritz Anschlag
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Fritz Anschlag took place on the night of January 26-27, 1888, when a crowd from around Garden Grove, California, pursued officers moving Anschlag, a German accused of murdering Charles B. Hitchcock and his wife, and broke into the Anaheim jail to seize him. Officers had hidden Anschlag and Antoine Decker, a hired man arrested with him, and took both to the Los Angeles county jail the next morning. Early wire dispatches wrongly reported that he had been hanged. He was later convicted and sentenced to death, and in November 1888 he poisoned himself in jail.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Fritz Anschlag and Antone Decker
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Fritz Anschlag and Antone Decker took place on the night of January 26, 1888, when a mob near Santa Ana, Los Angeles County, California, pursued two German prisoners accused of murdering Charles B. Hitchcock and his wife and broke open the Anaheim jail to seize them. Officers had moved the men ahead of the mob, and both were lodged in the Los Angeles county jail the next day. It drew national notice mainly because the first dispatches reported that Anschlag, or both men, had been lynched, a report withdrawn within a day.

episodes.title: Killing of Dr. Eady and capture of Baggott near Durango
episodes.lead: The killing of Dr. Eady and capture of Baggott near Durango took place in early January 1888, when an American named Baggott was accused of shooting Eady, an Englishman, over a disputed ranch, then escaped arrest and was recaptured by a posse. Wire reports from Nogales said the captured man would be shot, one copy said he had been shot, and a weekly news digest said he 'was lynched on the 4th'. No report describes a mob, and papers disagreed over whether the event took place in Arizona or Mexico.

episodes.title: Lynching of Ben Edwards
episodes.lead: The lynching of Ben Edwards took place at Amite City, Louisiana, on the night of January 28, 1888, when a body of about 100 armed men took Edwards, a Black man, from the town jail and hanged him to a tree. Edwards had been jailed on the accusation that he had criminally assaulted Catherine Hughes, a white girl who lived near the town. A dispatch from Amite City to the New Orleans Times-Democrat ran in papers from California to South Carolina, often under headlines such as "A Fiend Quickly Disposed Of."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Bob Yenders
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Bob Yenders took place in Rowan County, Kentucky, in late January 1888, when a number of farmers hanged Yenders from the beam above his cabin door on suspicion that he had raped a nine-year-old girl. He was cut down when word arrived that another man, John Hooper, was guilty, and one version says he survived. Papers across the country carried the story under headlines about the wrong man being hanged.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of eight Black youths at Camilla, Georgia
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of eight Black youths at Camilla, Georgia, followed a hearing on Monday, January 16, 1888, at which eight youths described as 'negro boys' faced a charge of criminal assault on a young white woman. Four of them were sent to jail to await trial, and the threats of lynching that followed came to nothing.

episodes.title: Lynching of David Dunce
episodes.lead: The lynching of David Dunce took place in late January 1888, when a mob took Dunce from the jail at a place the papers printed as Bell Green, Alabama, and lynched him. Dunce was held for the killing of W. R. Wilson at Russellville, Alabama, a few weeks earlier. The news travelled as a one-sentence telegraph item that ran in papers across the country within a week.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Dick Dent
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Dick Dent was a manhunt in Winchester, Ohio, at the end of January 1888, in which the white population searched for Dent, a Black man accused of seduction, and was reported ready to lynch him if he was caught. No report of his capture appears in the coverage, which consists of one wire dispatch reprinted in papers from Ohio to California.

episodes.title: Lynching of a sheepman in Harney Valley, Oregon (1888)
episodes.lead: The lynching of a sheepman in Harney Valley, Oregon, was a killing reported in early January 1888, in which an unnamed sheepman said to have killed a cattleman was himself lynched. A dispatch from The Dalles described the two deaths as a "double homicide" growing out of a quarrel between cattle and sheep men. The only known report is a two-sentence item in the Los Angeles Daily Herald, which gives no names, date or account of the lynchers.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Frank Wright
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Frank Wright took place in western Missouri in late January 1888, when a party of vigilantes took Wright, an accused horse thief, from the Benton County officer who had arrested him near Mayview. According to the Lexington Intelligencer, he narrowly escaped being hanged; the mob's part in the affair surfaced only in a single later clause of that paper's coverage of the Wright brothers.

episodes.title: Abduction of Henry Burney
episodes.lead: The abduction of Henry Burney was the removal of a Black prisoner from the Laurens County jail at Dublin, Georgia, by a party of masked men on the night of Tuesday, January 10, 1888. Burney was being held on a charge of knocking down and robbing J. M. Reinhart of Dublin. Georgia papers said only that he was believed, or possibly, lynched, while national news summaries reported flatly that he had been lynched, placing the event in Laurens County, Kentucky, or at Macon. A month later a Savannah paper reported that he had been sentenced to four years' imprisonment.

episodes.title: Hanging of Henry Harvey at Chico, Texas
episodes.lead: The hanging of Henry Harvey was an attempted lynching at Chico, Wise County, Texas, in late January or early February 1888, in which a party of twelve men took a prisoner accused of burglary from his guard and hanged him twice. He was cut down alive and later reported in jail, and the episode drew local condemnation and a promised grand jury inquiry.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Henry Wyman
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Henry Wyman took place on the evening of January 6, 1888, when a crowd at the Union Depot in Lansing, Michigan, tried to seize Wyman, a painter from Jackson, from officers taking him by train to the county jail at Mason. Wyman had been arrested on a charge of sexually assaulting an eight-year-old boy, and two officers held the crowd back at revolver point while state troops guarded the Mason jail overnight. A week later he was reported to have pleaded guilty, after fellow prisoners at Mason had prepared to hang him.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Louis Bulling and Peter Hronek
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Louis Bulling and Peter Hronek took place in St. Joseph, Missouri, in late January and early February 1888, when a mob and then a women's petition sought the lynching of two men held for killing their wives. Police hid Bulling from the mob, no attack on the jail was reported, and both men later went through the courts: Bulling was convicted of second-degree murder and Hronek was hanged legally. The petition, reported as the work of women weary of the law's delay, ran as a wire brief in papers across the country.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of James Semmes
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of James Semmes, also reported as Jim Seams, followed the shooting of a Tuscaloosa County deputy sheriff near Tuscaloosa, Alabama, on January 24, 1888. Semmes, a Black man the deputy had come to arrest on a warrant, was accused of killing him and escaped, and he was captured and wounded by the sheriff's posse three days later. According to a Birmingham dispatch, an effort to lynch him was made at Tuscaloosa, and the sheriff moved him to Birmingham under guard.

episodes.title: Killing of Jim Vance
episodes.lead: The killing of Jim Vance was the shooting of Jim (James) Vance, an older man linked to the Hatfield faction, by an armed party of Kentuckians in Logan County, West Virginia, in early January 1888. The party had come from Pike County, Kentucky, to hunt the Hatfields after a New Year's night raid on the home of Randolph McCoy, and later seized nine West Virginia men. Kentucky reports described a posse fighting the 'Hatfield gang', while West Virginia sources called the killing the murder of 'old man Vance' by men with no legal authority.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Joe Wooldridge
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Joe Wooldridge took place in Richmond, Virginia, on the evening of January 10, 1888, when an armed crowd pursued and fired on Wooldridge, a Black man accused of cutting a white youth, Emmet Branzell, in the abdomen. Wooldridge was wounded with birdshot, and according to the Richmond Dispatch the crowd called for a "rope" before police took him to the station-house. He was later indicted for the cutting, and in June 1888 a Hustings Court jury found him insane.

episodes.title: Lynching of John C. Wells
episodes.lead: The lynching of John C. Wells was the reported killing of a Canadian man at Bad Axe, Michigan, by friends of a neighbor whom Wells was said to have killed in a quarrel over a ditch. It was known to the press only through a wire telegram from Kingston, Ontario, in January 1888, which said the matter would be brought to the attention of the Dominion Government.

episodes.title: Lynching of Julian Medon
episodes.lead: The lynching of Julian Medon was the hanging of a young Mexican man whose body was found on a tree at Moore's Hill, eleven miles south of Mariposa, California, in late January 1888. The case drew renewed notice in July 1888, when three men were jailed as suspects in what a press dispatch called "plainly a case of lynching."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Lee Lung
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Lee Lung took place in Union Hill, New Jersey, on or about January 12, 1888, when a crowd gathered at the laundry of Lee Lung, a Chinese man, and prepared to lynch him after a seventeen-year-old girl accused him of attempting to assault her. A policeman sent to arrest him persuaded the crowd to desist, took him out by a rear door and brought him before the local recorder, who released him on $500 bail. Two New York papers reported the case the next morning, and a press dispatch carried it to the Pacific coast under the headline "A Mongolian Brute."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Louis Schlicht
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Louis Schlicht took place at Wausau, Wisconsin, on the night of January 1, 1888, when several hundred men surrounded the jail where Schlicht, a hotel keeper, was held for shooting Louis Butler. The crowd dispersed after Sheriff Healey warned that an armed posse would fire on any attempt, and Schlicht was later charged with first-degree murder. A wire report of the threatened lynching ran in papers from Minnesota to Texas.

episodes.title: Lynching of Patterson Spruill, John Blount and Matthew Blount
episodes.lead: The lynching of Patterson Spruill, John Blount and Matthew Blount took place near Plymouth, Washington County, North Carolina, on the night of January 26, 1888, when masked men took the three Black prisoners from the county jail and shot them to death. The men were awaiting trial for the murder of a traveling jeweler or peddler near Creswell. A Plymouth wire report carried the story to papers from Texas to Wisconsin, and a North Carolina editor called the lynchers murderers.

episodes.title: Plymouth triple lynching
episodes.lead: The Plymouth triple lynching was the killing of three Black prisoners, Matthew Blount, his brother Jack Blount and Patterson Spruill, by masked men at Plymouth, Washington County, North Carolina, around midnight on Thursday, January 26, 1888. Held on a charge of murdering a traveling peddler near Creswell, the men were taken from the jailer, tied to trees about a mile from town and shot to death. The killing was reported nationally by wire, a Raleigh correspondent called it the state's first lynching in many months, and no lyncher was identified.

episodes.title: Burning of Randall McCoy's house
episodes.lead: The burning of Randall McCoy's house was a night attack on McCoy's home on the Blackberry Fork of Pond Creek, Pike County, Kentucky, on or about January 1, 1888, in which attackers fired the house and shot the family as they came out. McCoy's daughter and a son were killed and his wife badly wounded; McCoy escaped. Papers across the country blamed the Hatfields of Logan County, West Virginia, as the latest act of the Hatfield-McCoy feud, though a Logan County state senator denied they took part.

episodes.title: Lynching of "Nosey" Smith
episodes.lead: The lynching of "Nosey" Smith was the hanging of a man by vigilantes at Sun River, Montana Territory, reported in January 1888. According to a dispatch from Macleod in the Northwest Territories, he was accused of having shamefully abused his two daughters and was hanged after returning to Montana to get them back. The brief item ran in papers from Virginia to Oregon, and a year-end tally later counted him among the year's victims of "Judge Lynch."

episodes.title: Lynching of old man Kelly
episodes.lead: The lynching of old man Kelly was the reported hanging of the elder member of the Kelly family of "No Man's Land" by pursuing vigilantes in the Texas Panhandle, described in dispatches dated January 2 to 4, 1888. According to these reports, the vigilantes overtook him after a long chase, hanged him, let him down until he confessed that his family had killed and robbed nine men and two women, and hanged him again. Papers from West Virginia to Montana ran it as the end of the Kelly murder case, but the Wichita Eagle called the Kelly stories "fabrications."

episodes.title: Caldwell jail lynching (1888)
episodes.lead: The Caldwell jail lynching was the shooting of Mexican prisoners in the jail at Caldwell, Texas, by a mob on the night of January 14 or 15, 1888. The prisoners were held on a charge of murdering a local planter, and at least one of them was killed. The Fort Worth Gazette reported one man dead and another dangerously wounded, while a Galveston wire and later news briefs spread the story nationally as the lynching of "two Mexican murderers."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Sam Price
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Sam Price took place at Clinton, Hickman County, Kentucky, in January 1888, when a crowd gathered to lynch Price, who was accused of killing Sheriff Henry Winter. Price had been captured in Tennessee and was not on the train the crowd met, so he was not harmed. The episode reached distant papers through short wire dispatches about his capture.

episodes.title: Madisonville lynchings (1888)
episodes.lead: The Madisonville lynchings were the killing of William "Bill" Bobo and the hanging of Reden S. "Red" Page by a body of several hundred armed citizens at Madisonville, the seat of Madison County, Texas, on January 3, 1888. They also fired on Alf Whitten and warned others to leave, and Governor Ross sent the Navasota Guards. Texas correspondents defended the killings as a rising against a gang of horse and cattle thieves, while a national wire report described "Reformers" killing men who favored saloons.

episodes.title: Lynching of Santos Salizer
episodes.lead: The lynching of Santos Salizer was the reported hanging of a Mexican man near Collins, in Nueces County, Texas, on the night of Sunday, January 22, 1888. He was accused of murdering Jacob Stafford, a sheep raiser whose body had been found in a water hole the day before. The story reached Corpus Christi only as a report, yet it ran in papers across the country, several of which headlined the slight evidence on which he was said to have been killed.

episodes.title: Limestone bank robbery lynching
episodes.lead: The Limestone bank robbery lynching was the reported hanging of an unnamed robber by a "Judge Lynch" court at Limestone, Indian Territory, in January 1888, after four masked men robbed the Citizens' Bank and killed its cashier, W. T. Reynolds. According to a widely reprinted despatch, a second robber, Thomas Evan, was shot dead in a gunfight with townspeople, and the two remaining robbers were sent to Fort Washita for the federal authorities. The story ran in papers from South Carolina to Wyoming, but a letter from Atoka printed in the Fort Worth Gazette said there had never been a bank, or a town, at Limestone Gap.

episodes.title: Warren settlement-dispute killings
episodes.lead: The Warren settlement-dispute killings were the reported killing of one Black man and the mortal wounding of another in Arkansas shortly before mid-January 1888, after a "squad" went to a Black man's house following a debt dispute with a white man named Gorman. The only account, a short item in an Arkansas news column, rested on rumor and named none of the dead, the wounded or the attackers.

episodes.title: Killing of William Dempsey
episodes.lead: The killing of William Dempsey took place in January 1888 near the mouth of Grapevine Creek in Logan County, West Virginia, when an armed party from Pike County, Kentucky, fired on a Logan County constable's posse in which Dempsey was serving. Dempsey was shot dead, and two accounts said he was finished off with a shot to the head as he lay wounded and pleading. The killing drew national coverage as part of the Hatfield-McCoy feud and led to indictments and rewards for the Kentucky party.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of A. J. Morris
episodes.lead: The reported lynching of A. J. Morris was the hanging, reported in wire briefs in February 1888, of a man accused of murdering Eugene Brusher, a Kansas cattleman, at Beaver City in No Man's Land. According to the brief, a mob captured Morris and hanged him to a rafter in the principal saloon of the town. Kansas papers closer to the scene said only that Morris had been arrested and "probably" lynched, and a later dispatch from Beaver City named a different killer, John Clark, who was tried and set free.

episodes.title: Lynching at Ponchatoula, 1888
episodes.lead: The lynching at Ponchatoula was the hanging of an unnamed Black man near Ponchatoula, Tangipahoa Parish, Louisiana, on the night of February 8, 1888. Accused of breaking into a white man's house and assaulting his young daughter, he was taken from officers who were bringing him to the parish jail and was hanged to a tree. A New Orleans dispatch counted it as the second lynching in Tangipahoa Parish within ten days, and the placard left on the body, "We Protect Our Women," served as the headline over the story in at least two papers.

episodes.title: Lynching of Alonzo Holly
episodes.lead: The lynching of Alonzo Holly took place at Pinckneyville, Perry County, Illinois, early on February 14, 1888, when masked men took Holly, a Black prisoner, from the county jail and hanged him from a tree nearby. Holly was held on a charge of assaulting a white woman near St. Johns. A Pinckneyville correspondent called it "the first lynching that ever occurred in Perry county," and wire dispatches carried it nationwide within a day.

episodes.title: Athens, Georgia, manhunt and lynching threat (1888)
episodes.lead: The Athens, Georgia, manhunt and lynching threat of February 1888 was a posse's search for an unnamed Black man accused of attempting to assault Miss O'Kelly, the daughter of a justice of the peace, near Athens. Residents declared that he would be lynched once caught, but the last report said he was still at large, and no outcome appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bill Reams and Sam Price
episodes.lead: The lynching of Bill Reams and Sam Price was the hanging of two jail prisoners, Reams, a Black man, and Price, a white man, by a mob at Clinton, Kentucky, on the night of February 27, 1888. Reams was accused of fatally shooting a man named Jackson who caught him stealing chickens, and Price of killing Hickman County sheriff Henry Winter. Wire reports carried the double lynching nationally, and a later dispatch drew notice by reporting that Price revived after being cut down and was hanged again.

episodes.title: Killing of Charlie Jackson
episodes.lead: The killing of Charlie Jackson was the fatal shooting of a Black man, named in reports as Charlie, Charles or Charley Jackson, by a constable's party of officers and citizens in Gonzales County, Texas, in February 1888, after he was accused of shooting the county's sheriff, Albert Little. Texas reports said Constable J. C. Nugent shot Jackson through the breast after Jackson fired at him, while a widely reprinted wire brief said Little had been killed and that a posse "riddled" Jackson with bullets. The first report from Luling also forecast that "Judge Lynch" would deal with Jackson that night, but no later report described a lynching.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Chastine Barker
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Chastine Barker was a threatened mob killing at Liberty, Virginia, around February 1, 1888, in which neighbors tried to lynch a white man arrested for assaulting a seven-year-old white girl. Officers held the crowd off with great difficulty, and Barker was lodged in jail. The episode reached southern papers through a single wire dispatch from Lynchburg.

episodes.title: Lynching at Gallup, New Mexico (1888)
episodes.lead: The lynching at Gallup, New Mexico, was the killing of an unnamed man by a mob at Gallup in early 1888, after he was accused of murdering one or both of his gambling companions. It is known from a single second-hand item, credited to the Optic and reprinted in the Arizona Silver Belt on February 25, 1888, which drew notice for the mob's use of a passenger coach's bell cord in place of a rope.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of George Robinson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of George Robinson took place in Frederick, Maryland, on the night of February 23, 1888, when an excited crowd tried to lynch a Black man who had just been arrested on an accusation of attempted assault at a hotel. Robinson was lodged in jail before the effort succeeded, and two days later he was bound over to the grand jury. The story ran briefly in white papers in Washington, Wilmington, Baltimore and Shepherdstown, under headlines that stressed the danger to the prisoner.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Harper Meadows
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Harper Meadows was a reported plan in February 1888 by citizens of Decker township, Illinois, to take Meadows from the jail at Fairfield and lynch him for the killing of Joseph F. Leavers. No report shows the mob reached the jail, and two months later Meadows was convicted of the murder and sentenced to fifty years in the penitentiary. The Olney dispatch announcing the mob ran in papers in Indiana, Tennessee, West Virginia, Kansas and Arkansas.

episodes.title: Reported Hinesville lynching of 1888
episodes.lead: The reported Hinesville lynching of 1888 was an account, carried by Georgia and Midwestern papers in February 1888, that armed men had seized a Black man accused of arson from a deputy sheriff in Liberty County, Georgia, and killed him. In November 1888 the Savannah Morning News reported that the lynching story had proved untrue and that the accused, George Washington, had been convicted of arson and sentenced to life.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of James Hughes
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of James Hughes took place at St. Ignace, Michigan, in February 1888, when a crowd went for Hughes, a lumberman accused of stealing a half dollar from the eye of a dead man. Officers kept him from harm, and he was held for trial. Papers from California to Virginia carried the story as a real case of the old saying about a man mean enough to steal from a dead man's eyes.

episodes.title: Killing of Jake Marshall, his brother and Louis Payton
episodes.lead: The killing of Jake Marshall, his brother and Louis Payton took place at Jeanerette, Louisiana, on or shortly before February 7, 1888, when 'unknown persons' shot the three men after Marshall, a Black deputy sheriff, had killed a man named George Dixon. Marshall's brother and Payton, a spectator, died almost at once, and Marshall's body was later found in a swamp ditch. A single special dispatch to the New Orleans Picayune carried the story to papers across the country under headlines counting 'four men' dead.

episodes.title: Shooting of Mack Henry and his wife
episodes.lead: The shooting of Mack Henry and his wife was an ambush in Florida on February 17, 1888, in which unknown parties fired buckshot at Henry, a one-armed Black man, at the door of his home, killing his wife and seriously wounding him. Henry survived, but a Lake City report in late July said he had been shot and killed by an unknown assassin at the same place.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Oscar Fifer
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Oscar Fifer took place at Athens, Tennessee, on February 25, 1888, when a crowd of Black residents surrounded the jail holding Fifer, a white man, hours after he shot and killed Matt Whiteside, described as a mulatto. According to a Chattanooga dispatch, the crowd said it would lynch Fifer before morning, but no report of what followed appears in the coverage. The story reached readers mainly through a brief wire item in Richmond and Savannah papers.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of the Porter burglary suspects, Lawrenceville, Illinois
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of the Porter burglary suspects took place at Lawrenceville, Illinois, in February 1888, when a crowd of 'vigilants' gathered as four men accused of nearly killing a farmer and his wife were brought to the county jail. Sheriff Lee Gowens and his deputies brought the prisoners in at midnight under a strong guard, and the crowd made only a 'slight demonstration.' A week later a Lawrenceville dispatch reported that the four had been indicted and sentenced to ten years each.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of George Tippett
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of George Tippett took place in February 1888 in Panola County, Texas, after Tippett, a Black barber, was jailed at Carthage when silver dollars from the robbery and murder of County Treasurer D. C. Hill were found buried at his home. Fears that he would be lynched were reported while he was held, and a later wire dispatch said he had "narrowly escaped being lynched." Suspicion then shifted to Tom Forsyth, the sheriff's son, who confessed to the murder and was himself hanged by a crowd, and wire reports said Forsyth had planted the money in the barber's yard.

episodes.title: Lynching of Tom Forsythe
episodes.lead: The lynching of Tom Forsythe took place at Carthage, Panola County, Texas, on the night of February 28-29, 1888, when about 400 men took the sheriff's son from jail and hanged him. Forsythe had been arrested days earlier and was reported to have confessed to the murder and robbery of County Treasurer D. C. Hill. The case drew notice because the lynchers acted unmasked and laid the body in the victim's blood, and because Governor Ross rebuked them.

episodes.title: Death of an unidentified man in the Boston Mountains, Arkansas (1888)
episodes.lead: In February 1888 two hunters found the body of an unidentified, heavily armed man in the Boston Mountains of Arkansas, near a still where a revenue collector had killed its owner the previous fall. No marks showed how he died, but newspapers supposed he was a detective gathering evidence against illicit distilling and headlined the death "Murdered by Moonshiners."

episodes.title: Coal Hill convict camp killings
episodes.lead: The Coal Hill convict camp killings were the deaths of Charles Williams, a Black convict, and other prisoners at a leased-convict coal-mining camp at Coal Hill, Johnson County, Arkansas, in early 1888. A coroner's jury found that Williams died from a whipping by the camp warden, J. A. Gafford, who fled, was indicted and was captured in Tennessee that November. The revelations led residents to threaten to hang the warden, prompted a state penitentiary board investigation, and were carried by papers across the country.

episodes.title: Spanish Camp massacre
episodes.lead: The Spanish Camp massacre was the killing of Black residents at Spanish Camp, Wharton County, Texas, early on Sunday, February 26, 1888, when attackers fired a cabin and shot its occupants as they fled. Later reports put the dead at seven of the eight people inside, and the body of a Black man, William Battle, was found hanging nearby. The killings, traced to a land suit the Black residents had won, drew national wire coverage, a Texas editorial dispute over the governor's response, arrests, and mention in the United States Senate.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Zeph Davis
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Zeph Davis took place at Forest, Illinois, a Wabash railroad station about sixty miles south of Chicago, on February 28, 1888, when a crowd of farmers tried to seize Davis, a young man the papers called a "mulatto," from the marshal who had captured him. Davis was accused of killing fifteen-year-old Maggie Gaughan in a Chicago factory the day before; the marshal kept him from the crowd until a train carried him back to the city. The New York Sun printed the only detailed account of the scene at Forest, while other dispatches said only that Davis "narrowly escaped lynching in the country."

episodes.title: Lynching of Aaron Dickey
episodes.lead: The lynching of Aaron Dickey took place at Bluffton, Georgia, shortly before March 4, 1888, when a party of young men tied Dickey, a Black man, to a tree and whipped him until he died. The men acted on the suspicion that Dickey was intimate with a white woman, and a dispatch from Cuthbert that ran in papers from Connecticut to Nevada called the killing "the execution of popular vengeance."

episodes.title: Killing of Albert West
episodes.lead: The killing of Albert West was the fatal shooting of a young Black prisoner by a guard at the Indianapolis work-house on March 2, 1888. The guard, Stewart, said West had attacked him with stones and fractured his skull before he fired, and that version, drawn from his own ante-mortem statement, was the only one the papers printed. The Indianapolis Journal gave the case a long local account, while a short wire dispatch carried it to papers from Kansas to New York and weekly digests repeated it through March.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Alfred Lewis
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Alfred Lewis took place at Barnum, Minnesota, in March 1888, after Lewis, a Black restaurant keeper, was jailed on an accusation of killing Frank Burke. The St. Paul Daily Globe reported the threat but described no crowd or attempt, and a week later found Lewis still in jail, claiming self-defense.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of the Blalock brothers
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of the Blalock brothers took place at Columbus, Kansas, in March 1888, when crowds threatened to lynch William and John Blalock after their capture for the killing of Constable David Gordon. Officials calmed the crowd and guarded the prisoners, and the brothers were later tried and sentenced to life. Papers across the country treated the case as notable chiefly because the family's daughter, a local school teacher, was named as a leader of a gang of thieves.

episodes.title: Lynching of Charles Duncan
episodes.lead: The lynching of Charles Duncan took place in McDowell County, West Virginia, in early March 1888, when a mob took Duncan from officers who were carrying him to jail and hanged him to a tree. Duncan had been accused of shooting Milt Hawks, the man he lived with, during a quarrel between Hawks and his wife. A Parkersburg dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, and the Evening Star of Washington predicted that nothing would be done about it.

episodes.title: Lynching of Eli Davie
episodes.lead: The lynching of Eli Davie was the killing of a Black man, charged with burning a tobacco barn near Fulton, Kentucky, who was taken from a train by masked men at Woodland Mills, Obion County, Tennessee, early on March 15, 1888, and hanged. He was in the custody of a constable who was carrying him to the county jail at Hickman, Kentucky, after an examining trial at Fulton, where open threats to lynch him had been made. A coroner's jury found death at the hands of unknown parties, and a Union City dispatch carried the story from Indiana to California.

episodes.title: Charles Mix County wife-murder lynching pursuit
episodes.lead: The Charles Mix County wife-murder lynching pursuit was a reported attempt in March 1888 by a party in Charles Mix County, Dakota Territory, to hunt down and lynch a man said to have murdered his wife. No lynching was reported, and about a week later a man accused of a wife murder in the county was reported under arrest at Wheeler.

episodes.title: Lynching near Australia Landing, Mississippi (1888)
episodes.lead: The lynching near Australia Landing, Mississippi, was the hanging of an unnamed Black man by a mob of Black men on a plantation in Bolivar County in late March 1888. He had been accused of killing or wounding a popular man during a quarrel at a plantation ball, and friends of the slain man took him and hanged him to a tree on the Mississippi River levee. Memphis reports carried the story to papers in Kentucky and South Carolina, where one account presented it as the work of a 'Band of Black Ku-Klux'.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of F. G. Polanski
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of F. G. Polanski took place at Barnesville, Minnesota, on the night of Thursday, March 29, 1888, when armed men broke into the town jail and carried off Polanski, a hardware merchant held on his wife's complaint of assault. Armed officers and a posse of citizens rescued him before he was harmed, and the short dispatch describing the averted "lynching bee" ran in papers from Connecticut to Dakota Territory.

episodes.title: Killing of Gaither Reese
episodes.lead: The killing of Gaither Reese was the fatal shooting of Reese, of Spring Creek in Madison County, North Carolina, in March 1888 by a party of Haywood County men led by Jerome Ruff, who were trying to arrest him on a Haywood capias. Four men were indicted for murder, the case was moved to Buncombe County and continued, and Ruff remained at large under a $200 reward offered by the governor. The Asheville Citizen called it "a horrible murder" and argued that an officer had no right to shoot a man accused only of a misdemeanor who tried to escape.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of George Crisp
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of George Crisp was a series of threats in March and May 1888 by residents of Coal Hill, Arkansas, a mining camp, to lynch Crisp, who was jailed at Ozark charged with criminal assault on the eight-year-old daughter of a Coal Hill minister. In March a St. Louis dispatch forecast "a double lynching" of Crisp and of Clifford, a penitentiary warden accused of brutality to convicts. In May about thirty armed men seized a switch engine to go to Ozark for Crisp, but the party broke up in a dispute before leaving, and no report says Crisp was harmed.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of George Mitchell
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of George Mitchell took place on Sunday afternoon, March 18, 1888, near the Virginia end of the Aqueduct bridge in Alexandria County, Virginia, when a large crowd threatened to lynch Mitchell, a Black county constable, after he shot Roger Fields, a young white man from Washington. Mitchell was hidden in a nearby stable guarded by a bulldog and later escaped, and no one was reported hurt by the crowd. Washington, Alexandria and Richmond papers disagreed over whether Mitchell had provoked the fight or fired in self-defense.

episodes.title: Killing of Archie Stokes at the Woodlawn road convict camp
episodes.lead: The killing of Archie Stokes at the Woodlawn road convict camp took place on the morning of March 24, 1888, near Birmingham, Alabama, when deputy sheriffs fired on a squad of leased county convicts who had refused to work. Stokes, a Black convict, was killed and a second convict, Henry Allen, was wounded, and a coroner's jury found the shooting was done in performance of duty. Papers around the country carried the story as the suppression of a convict "mutiny".

episodes.title: Rumored lynching of Homer and Oliver Hart
episodes.lead: The rumored lynching of Homer and Oliver Hart was a report, sent from Detroit on the night of March 4, 1888, that a father and son from Mount Pleasant, Michigan, arrested on a charge of criminally assaulting the son's five-year-old daughter, had been lynched. The rumor came without particulars and was reprinted in papers across the country, some of which headlined it as fact. No confirmation or denial appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Killing of Hunley Royl
episodes.lead: The killing of Hunley Royl was the assassination of an elderly Black man living near Newport, Arkansas, by a party of masked men, reported in early March 1888. The only account found is a single line in a weekly state news column, which gave no date, motive or follow-up.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of J. A. Gafford
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of J. A. Gafford was a threat by residents of Coal Hill, Arkansas, in March 1888 to hang the warden of the town's convict mining camp after an inquest blamed him for the deaths of convicts. No attempt on him was reported; he fled, was captured in November and was convicted of second-degree murder at Clarksville in December. The threat reached the national press as the closing line of wire stories about convict abuse, and a later dispatch forecast a "double lynching" that did not take place.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of James Derossett
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of James Derossett was a failed mob attempt in late March 1888 to take Derossett, who was charged with killing a man named Smith near Dayton, Tennessee, from the Dayton jail and hang him. The sheriff removed the prisoner before the mob reached him, and no injury to Derossett was reported. The episode reached readers in several Southern states through short telegraphic briefs that disagreed on the dead man's first name and on where Derossett was taken.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jeff Curry
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jeff Curry was the killing of a Black man who was taken from two officers escorting him to jail in Birmingham, Alabama, and shot dead on the road in March 1888. Wire reports placed the killing on Sunday night, March 18, after a dispute with a white man named Powell led to Curry's arrest. Within a week four white men, among them Powell and men who had Curry in charge, were jailed as his murderers, and one paper called it the first time in the state that white men had been held for lynching a Black man.

episodes.title: Killing of Jim Harrington
episodes.lead: The killing of Jim Harrington was the shooting of a Black farm worker by four masked men near Farmerville, Louisiana, on the evening of Friday, March 30, 1888. The men took him from the field where he was plowing, led him into the Loutre swamp with a rope around his neck, and shot him; a coroner's investigation could not identify them. The local paper called it "a murder surrounded with mystery."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Joe Nebares
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Joe Nebares took place in Waco, Texas, on March 24, 1888, when an excited mob gathered after Nebares, a barber, was jailed on an accusation of attempting to rape his ten-year-old stepdaughter. According to a Waco telegram, only the steel bars of his cell saved him from being lynched, and the Austin Weekly Statesman printed the story under the headline "Almost a Lynching." He remained in custody and was indicted by a grand jury within days.

episodes.title: Killing of George Madden and the Winona lynching mob
episodes.lead: The killing of George Madden and the Winona lynching mob was an episode of mob violence at Winona, Shannon County, Missouri, in early March 1888, in which railroad laborers hunted Constable John Rucker after he was reported to have shot and killed the subcontractor George Madden. No report of Rucker's fate appears in the coverage, and a single Springfield dispatch said the laborers caught and lynched two of his friends and shot a third. Most papers carried the story as a St. Louis wire report of an "atrocious murder" followed by a "howling mob."

episodes.title: Lynching of John Skinner
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Skinner was the hanging of a Black prisoner by masked men who took him from the jail at Hopkinsville, Kentucky, early on Wednesday, March 14, 1888. Skinner was held on a charge of shooting Ballard Fourqurean the previous November, and the mob hanged him from a wild cherry tree near the spot of that shooting. A coroner's jury found death 'by parties unknown,' and the circuit judge directed the grand jury to indict the lynchers for murder.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Slater
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John Slater took place on the morning of 4 March 1888 in Jefferson, a suburb northwest of Chicago, when a crowd of neighbors armed with clubs, stones and a rope pursued the one-armed policeman after a wounded saloonkeeper's words were taken to accuse him of shooting. Slater, then under arrest, escaped when a police lieutenant turned his buggy and drove him to a station house. He was cleared within hours, and newspapers across the country told the story as the narrow escape of an innocent man.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Wood
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Wood was the reported killing of a Black man at Denison, Texas, on March 28, 1888. Wood was accused of abducting Amelia Wilson, described as a white girl, and was said to have been lynched for it. The case reached readers only as a one-sentence wire item and as a line in a year-end roll of lynching victims.

episodes.title: Cherokee Strip squatter killings
episodes.lead: The Cherokee Strip squatter killings were the killing of three settlers, named in the first reports as Julius Quinn, William Antwerp and Joseph George, by cowboys of the cattleman George H. Delaney in the Cherokee Strip of the Indian Territory in early March 1888. Wichita dispatches said the men were burned out of their cabin and shot; a deputy U.S. marshal's account added a woman and a cowboy to the dead. The story ran nationally, and later dispatches reported two cattlemen lynched in reprisal.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of two cattlemen in the Cherokee Strip
episodes.lead: The reported lynching of two cattlemen in the Cherokee Strip was the reported killing of two men said to belong to cattleman George H. Delaney's band of cowboys at the hands of settlers near the line of No Man's Land, Indian Territory, in March 1888. Papers presented it as retribution for the killing of three squatters on Delaney's range a few days earlier. The lynching was carried only as a report from Wichita and Woodward, and the men were never named.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Lemuel Ogden
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Lemuel Ogden took place in March 1888 in Prince George's County, Maryland, when neighbors of the Fowler family talked of lynching Ogden, a white man charged with assaulting his sister-in-law, and tried to organize a party to visit the Marlboro' jail. No attack on the jail was reported, and Ogden was tried in April, found guilty and sentenced to 18 years in the penitentiary.

episodes.title: Killing of Margaret Auxier
episodes.lead: The killing of Margaret Auxier was the shooting death of a young woman by a party of men at her father's house near Yocum, Morgan County, Kentucky, in early March 1888. Several men were held on suspicion and lynching was talked of, and in August a man charged with the crime was himself found murdered after saying he would turn State's evidence.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching at Barnesville, Minnesota
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching at Barnesville, Minnesota, took place in late March 1888, when an armed mob broke into the town jail and carried off a man held on his wife's complaint of assault. The man, whose name was printed as Polenski, Poliuski and Polanski, survived without harm. Reports disagree on how he escaped: one says the mob relented when he begged for his life, the other that officers and citizens rescued him.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Rafe Bird
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Rafe Bird took place near Pooler, Georgia, on the night of March 27, 1888, when armed men from Pooler took Bird, a Black farmer suspected in the killing of Joseph Gill, into a swamp and threatened to lynch him unless he talked. Under the threat he accused a Black man named Brown, who was seized and then released; Bird was jailed in Savannah and freed in July when a grand jury declined to indict him. The Savannah Morning News reported the episode within its running coverage of the Gill murder under the headline words "His Narrow Escape from Lynching."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Robert Hardin
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Robert Hardin was a pursuit in March 1888 of a young Black school teacher near Utica, Kentucky, by a posse or "lynching party" bent on lynching him. Hardin was accused of seducing his pupil Amanda Pry and other girls in his school and of causing Pry's death by an attempted abortion, and he fled before he could be arrested. No report in the coverage says the pursuers found him.

episodes.title: Lynching of Slume and Jonninna
episodes.lead: The lynching of Slume and Jonninna was the hanging of two Kootenai men by a party of white settlers on the east bank of the Flathead River, opposite Demersville in Missoula County, Montana Territory, in March 1888. The settlers accused the two, with a third Kootenai named Antley who escaped, of killing three prospectors on Wolf Creek the previous summer. The hanging set off a scare of a Kootenai uprising, a petition for federal troops and wire coverage across the country.

episodes.title: Killing of two Black men near Spanish Camp, Texas (March 1888)
episodes.lead: The killing of two Black men near Spanish Camp, Texas, took place on a plantation in Wharton County in the third week of March 1888, a few weeks after a massacre of Black residents at the same settlement. The victims were not named and no one was reported arrested. Papers treated the killings as fresh proof of a 'reign of terror' against the county's Black population that state rangers had failed to stop.

episodes.title: Lynching of Theo Calloway
episodes.lead: The lynching of Theo Calloway was the killing of a Black man accused of murdering a white man, Mitchell Gresham, by about 200 armed and masked men who took him from the Lowndes County jail at Hayneville, Alabama, on the night of March 29, 1888, and hanged him in front of the courthouse. A Montgomery dispatch about the lynching ran in papers from Maine to Texas within a week, and the Huntsville Gazette called it "shameful" and urged punishment of the mob. In May, reports of an armed clash between the county sheriff's posse and Black residents traced the trouble to the lynching.

episodes.title: Lynching of Tom Roof
episodes.lead: The lynching of Tom Roof took place in Trenton, Georgia, in March 1888, when a mob took a Black man accused of an attempted assault on Mrs. Joseph Morrison from the county jail and hanged him in the public square. Papers across the country carried the story, giving the man's name variously as Roof, Root, Poof and Ruffin. Much of the coverage turned on one wire's claim that the mob "consisted mostly of women."

episodes.title: Killing of an unnamed Black man near Australia Landing (1888)
episodes.lead: The killing of an unnamed Black man near Australia Landing was a fatal shooting in March 1888 on the Sledge and Mason plantations, a few miles below Australia Landing, in which Robert Taylor, a white man, shot and killed a Black man who, according to the only report, had attempted to strike him. The shooting reached the press only as a single sentence in a Memphis dispatch that was mainly about a lynching on the same plantations.

episodes.title: Lynching of Will Thomas
episodes.lead: The lynching of Will Thomas was the hanging of a Black man by a band of about forty armed "regulators" at Tunnel Hill, Georgia, on the evening of March 9, 1888. Thomas was accused of assaulting Mrs. Eliza Anderson, a widow, the day before, and was hanged to a tree after she identified him. Papers across the country carried the Chattanooga dispatches, several stressing that the woman had asked to shoot him and been refused.

episodes.title: Lynching of William A. Parker
episodes.lead: The lynching of William A. Parker was the hanging of a white man by masked men from the river drawbridge at Washington, North Carolina, in March 1888, after they took him from the town lock-up. Parker had been tried and acquitted in the 1880 assassination of Gen. Bryan Grimes, and his killers left a placard reading "Justice at last." A coroner's jury blamed persons unknown, and papers as far away as Minnesota called him Grimes's murderer.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Price
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of William Price took place at Higginsville, Lafayette County, Missouri, in early March 1888, when, after Price, a Black man, was accused of cutting another man's neck in a saloon fight, there was talk among residents of lynching him. Officers quickly took Price out of town to the jail at Lexington, and no attempt on him was reported.

episodes.title: Bloodhound pursuit and hanging near Birmingham (Detroit Free Press sketch)
episodes.lead: The bloodhound pursuit and hanging near Birmingham is an incident described in a first-person sketch from the Detroit Free Press, reprinted in April 1888, in which an unnamed Black man was run down by hounds, hanged from a tree limb and shot beside a railroad siding. The leader of the party that killed him said only that he had assaulted a white woman near Birmingham; the sketch gives no date, name or state.

episodes.title: 1888 Globe jail raid
episodes.lead: The 1888 Globe jail raid was a failed attempt by six masked men to break into the county jail at Globe, Arizona Territory, early on April 13, 1888, and take out two prisoners, Thomas Burns and Harry Blevins. The men fled when the prisoners raised a cry, and no one was hurt. Outside papers reported it as a foiled lynching, while the local paper said it was unknown whether the raiders meant to lynch or free the prisoners.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Stephen Clutts
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Stephen Clutts was a threat by a mob against a man held at Marion, Williamson County, Illinois, in April 1888 on a charge of murdering his wife. A lynching party was organized on a Monday night, but the sheriff moved Clutts to the Johnson County jail before it acted. Two papers outside Illinois noted the case in short items, one calling the killing among the most brutal in the county's history.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of the Corbett brothers
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of the Corbett brothers took place in south Florida in the spring of 1888, when De Soto county stock owners seized the brothers at home on a charge of cattle theft and put ropes around their necks. After one brother was pulled off the ground, the stockmen gave them ten days to leave the country or hang.

episodes.title: Killing of the "Scar Face" horse-thief gang, 1888
episodes.lead: The killing of the "Scar Face" horse-thief gang was the pursuit and killing of a band of accused horse thieves by a farmers' vigilance committee in the Indian Territory in April 1888. Reports said that about eight members of the gang died, three of them killed after capture, and that one vigilante was shot dead. Papers nationwide called it a mass lynching; one California paper condemned killing men who had surrendered.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of David Bell
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of David Bell took place at Marshall, Madison County, North Carolina, in April 1888, when a mob of about one hundred men gathered at the county jail to lynch Bell, who was held on a charge of assaulting a married woman. The sheriff removed Bell from the jail by a ruse and took him to Asheville, and Bell was later tried, convicted and sentenced to death. A Knoxville wire story about the attempt ran in papers as far away as Kansas and Arkansas.

episodes.title: Killing of W. E. Ashley and Eugene Grove
episodes.lead: The killing of W. E. Ashley and Eugene Grove was the hanging of Grove and shooting of Ashley, two men from Belvidere, Kansas, by a band of vigilantes a few miles below Englewood in the Indian Territory, reported in late April 1888. Grove was hanged at the vigilantes' camp and Ashley was shot dead after he opened fire, while two women travelling with them were never accounted for. A single Belvidere dispatch carried the story from Washington to the Kansas weeklies, and its closing judgment that vigilantes were "worse than those whom they seek to kill" made it a small case against frontier vigilantism.

episodes.title: Shooting into the Essex Dargan house
episodes.lead: The shooting into the Essex Dargan house took place near Bennettsville, in Marlboro County, South Carolina, at the end of April 1888, when a number of men fired into the home of a Black man whose son was jailed for killing a white youth and killed a three-year-old child. The son, Dock Dargan, was not harmed by the men; a wire dispatch said several attempts had been made to lynch him, while the local paper spoke only of rumors. He was hanged at Bennettsville that September.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching and banishment of Doe Moran
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching and banishment of Doe Moran took place in Stanford, Kentucky, on Sunday, April 1, 1888, when a Black man accused of writing a note to a young woman was seized by the town marshal and threatened with lynching. He was released on condition that he leave and never return, and he left at once. The only known account is a short item in the local Semi-Weekly Interior Journal, which approved of the outcome.

episodes.title: Killing of E. L. Little
episodes.lead: The killing of E. L. Little was the fatal shooting of a Black preacher by the city marshal of Conway, Arkansas, in April 1888. According to a dispatch from Conway, City Marshal John H. Howard shot Little after the preacher knocked him down with a can of peaches, and the story ran as a brief in papers from Texas to Rhode Island over the following three weeks. Other reports gave different names and causes for the quarrel.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Ed Chamberlain
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Ed Chamberlain took place at Delphi, Carroll County, Indiana, on the night of April 28, 1888, when rumors spread that a mob from White County would storm the jail holding Chamberlain, who was accused of fatally shooting a young woman at Reynolds. Shortly before midnight the Carroll County sheriff and an armed posse took the prisoner out of the jail and drove him to Lafayette, and no attack was made. A second lynching threat followed in late May at Monticello, after Chamberlain was accused of beating the White County sheriff during a jail escape, and state militia guarded the jail. Chamberlain was never lynched; he hanged himself in jail at Logansport on December 3, 1888, in the middle of his murder trial.

episodes.title: Lynching in Claiborne County, Mississippi (1888)
episodes.lead: The lynching in Claiborne County, Mississippi, was the punishment of an unnamed Black man accused of rape by "Judge Lynch" in the week before May 5, 1888. It is known from a single sentence in the Grenada Sentinel, which paired it with a lynching at Vicksburg and did not say what was done to the man.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of John J. Farris
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of John J. Farris occurred on the night of April 19, 1888, when a crowd gathered at Lewistown, Illinois, intending to take Farris from the Fulton County jail and hang him for the murder of Stephen McGehee. Finding the jail under armed guard, the crowd withdrew, and Sheriff Smith drove the prisoner overnight to Cuba and took him by train to the jail at Peoria. Farris was later tried at Peoria on a change of venue and sentenced to hang.

episodes.title: Killing of a Black child near Fort Smith (1888)
episodes.lead: The killing of a Black child near Fort Smith was the fatal shooting of an unnamed boy of about four on the porch of a roadside house about ten miles out of Fort Smith, Arkansas, on the road to the Choctaw Nation, Indian Territory, on April 12, 1888. One of two drunken men driving home from Fort Smith fired at the boy as they passed, and a deputy marshal arrested both men the same day. Newspapers across the country reprinted the story as an example of wanton cruelty, and a Fort Smith dispatch called it one of the most horrible murders in the Indian Territory.

episodes.title: Lynching of Joseph Prescott
episodes.lead: The lynching of Joseph Prescott was the fatal shooting of a Black man by a band of white "regulators" in southeastern Pike County, Mississippi, near Dillon's Bridge, after midnight on the night of Sunday, April 8, 1888. The same band reportedly beat Frank Warner, a Black boy of about fifteen, into accusing Prescott and the brothers Hardy and Ben Kaigler of trying to rob a store, then whipped the Kaiglers. A coroner's jury charged twenty-four white men and seventeen were arrested, while residents near the scene publicly disputed the Magnolia Gazette's account.

episodes.title: Lynching of Franklin Baker
episodes.lead: The lynching of Franklin Baker was the hanging of a Colorado homesteader by a mob at Cheyenne Wells in April 1888, after he was arrested for shooting two land seekers who crossed his claim. Officers were moving him toward Denver when the mob, put at fifty men, took him and hanged him to a railroad coal chute. The case ran in papers from Washington to California, first as a shooting and a promised lynching, then as brief notices of the hanging.

episodes.title: Lynching of George Montgomery
episodes.lead: The lynching of George Montgomery was the hanging of a man accused of horse stealing by a vigilance committee of Kansas and No Man's Land settlers at Neutral City, No Man's Land, on Sunday, April 8, 1888. According to an account carried by the Wichita Eagle, Montgomery was captured with four horses said to be stolen, was said to have confessed, and was hanged before seventy-five or one hundred men. Wire specials from Woodward and Oklahoma, Indian Territory, instead told of Kansas farmers hanging four horse thieves and besieging the rest of their band, so the reports disagree on how many died.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of George Starkweather
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of George Starkweather took place on 12 April 1888, when a crowd of citizens seized the 60-year-old wood chopper from a justice's office in Pennsylvania and put a rope around his neck. A sheriff's posse rescued him and took him to the jail at Garland. Papers across the country carried the Titusville wire dispatch, several under headlines regretting that he had escaped.

episodes.title: Killing of Billy Gill
episodes.lead: The killing of Billy Gill took place in the Indian Territory near Woodward about April 6, 1888, when a party of some two dozen men from southern Kansas pursued Gill, whom they accused of stealing their horses, and shot him dead. No arrest or inquest was reported. Papers from Kansas to Georgia carried the news, treating Gill as a notorious desperado, and one dispatch linked his killers to vigilance committees that meant to execute horse thieves without trial.

episodes.title: Lynching of Hardy Posey
episodes.lead: The lynching of Hardy Posey took place at Bessemer, Alabama, around midnight on April 23, 1888, when masked men took Posey, a Black man accused of attempting to rape a young white girl, from the town marshal and hanged him near the railroad depot. A placard on the body, signed "Bessemer's Best," declared that "our mothers, wives and daughters must and shall be protected." Telegraph reports that Black residents had risen to burn the town in revenge carried the story nationally, though next-day dispatches called the alarm exaggerated.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Pope
episodes.lead: The lynching of Henry Pope took place at Summerville, Chattooga county, Georgia, on the night of April 30-May 1, 1888, when a mob of about fifty masked men took Pope, a Black prisoner, from the county jail and hanged him from the court-house banisters. Pope had twice been convicted of assaulting a young white woman, Minnie Kendrick, and had been respited by Governor Gordon days before his scheduled execution on evidence that he had been in Alabama at the time. The killing was reported across the country, and one Atlanta dispatch called Pope an innocent man.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Pope
episodes.lead: The lynching of Henry Pope took place at Summerville, Chattooga County, Georgia, on the night of April 30, 1888, when about fifty masked men took Pope, a Black man, from the county jail and hanged him from the courthouse banisters. Pope had twice been convicted of assaulting a young white woman, but Governor Gordon had just respited him on evidence that he had been in Alabama that day. Wire briefs called him a "rapist," while an Atlanta dispatch printed in Wheeling and several Northern papers treated the case as the hanging of a probably innocent man.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bill Parkman
episodes.lead: The lynching of Bill Parkman was the killing of a Black prisoner accused of burglary, taken with Henry Williams from his guards at Raleigh, Meriwether County, Georgia, in April 1888 by fifteen or twenty armed men. Parkman's beaten and burned body was found the next morning near Cane Creek. Williams, at first reported lynched too, turned up alive days later.

episodes.title: Lynching of Isaac and Puss Kirkpatrick
episodes.lead: The lynching of Isaac and Puss Kirkpatrick was the killing of a Black ("colored") married couple by a mob near Gallatin, Tennessee, about midnight on April 18, 1888, in which the wife was hanged and the husband shot. Puss Kirkpatrick had been suspected of burning a nearby country house, while her husband, who was not suspected, was believed to have been killed because he recognized members of the mob. A wire dispatch carried the story across the country within a day, and several Northern and Western papers printed it under headlines condemning mob law.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Will Collins
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Will Collins took place in Wilkinson County, Georgia, in April 1888, after Collins, a Black man, was accused of shooting and robbing J. A. Sheffield, a merchant of Irwinton. Townspeople tracked and captured him, and Sheriff Fountain took him to Macon to prevent a lynching. Collins was not harmed; in October 1888 a jury at Irwinton found him guilty of murder.

episodes.title: Lynching of J. H. Howe
episodes.lead: The lynching of J. H. Howe took place at Fort Collins, Colorado, on the night of April 4, 1888, when a mob took Howe from the county jail and hanged him from a builders' derrick, hours after his arrest for killing his wife. Wire reports carried the story nationally, and a Denver Republican correspondent reported that doctors, lawyers and clergymen attended and that the town approved.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jerry Smith
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jerry Smith was the hanging of a Black man by a group of men at Tiptonville, Lake county, Tennessee, in April 1888, while he was being held in jail on an accusation of attempted rape. Smith was taken from jail on the morning his case was to come before the court and was found hanging from a tree near the river bank. A Memphis wire carried the news across the country in two lines, and no one was identified as taking part.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jim Harris
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jim Harris was the killing of a Black man at Vicksburg, Mississippi, on the night of April 30, 1888, by men a Mississippi weekly described only as "citizens." Harris had been accused of criminally assaulting a white woman, Mrs. M. Simmons, the night before, and he refused to confess before he was killed. A New Orleans Picayune dispatch carried the case to papers from Georgia to Dakota, while Mississippi papers added that he was hanged at the courthouse door and that officials were criticized for trying to save a white accomplice.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of J. T. Wolck
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of J. T. Wolck took place on April 9, 1888, when about forty workmen at the H. F. Shufeldt & Co. distillery in Chicago seized a private detective, also named as John T. Walck, and put a rope around his neck, saying he was spying for the whisky trust. Thomas Lynch, a partner in the firm, stopped the hanging, and the detective was tied to a post, made to swear a statement before a notary public, and driven into the street. Papers across the country carried it as a sidelight on the trust's campaign against an independent distillery.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Lee McElroy
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Lee McElroy was a mob's attempt in Louisville, Kentucky, in April 1888 to lynch a 15-year-old Black youth accused of carrying off a young white child to hold for ransom. Police held off the crowd, and McElroy was taken to jail alive. A Louisville wire story carried the case to papers from New York and Washington to Utah, Kansas and Wyoming, most of them saying that only his youth had kept him from being lynched.

episodes.title: Lima jail mob of 1888
episodes.lead: The Lima jail mob of 1888 was an attempt by a white crowd to lynch Black men accused of a fatal stabbing in Lima, Ohio, on the night of the city election, April 2, 1888. The mob, put at 500 to two thousand, forced its way into the county jail, beat Lew Hunter and opened every cell, but officers had hidden the accused and no one was lynched. Papers from New Hampshire to Mississippi carried the story, much of it as a wire report that overstated the deaths in the fight.

episodes.title: Shawneetown horse thieves shootout
episodes.lead: The Shawneetown horse thieves shootout was a gunfight near Shawneetown, Indian Territory, reported on April 10, 1888, in which a deputy United States marshal and Sac and Fox Indian police pursued three Black men accused of stealing horses from a Shawnee man named Long Tom. Two of the accused men and one Indian policeman were reported killed and the marshal badly wounded, though one condensed copy of the dispatch put the police dead at two. The story ran widely as a telegraph item, and a longer version joined it to a lynching of horse thieves on the Kansas border that another dispatch reported separately.

episodes.title: Healdton lynchings (1888)
episodes.lead: The Healdton lynchings were the hanging of Bill Morgan and two or three other men by a mob of citizens near Healdton, in the Chickasaw Nation of Indian Territory, on the night of Monday, April 9, 1888. The men were accused of belonging to a band of horse thieves, and federal deputy marshals afterward arrested some of those said to have been in the mob. Newspapers in Texas and across the country carried the news from Gainesville, Texas, and the case was later entered in year-end tallies of lynchings.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Manny Sidebottom
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Manny Sidebottom took place at Somerset, Kentucky, in April 1888, when a mob gathered to lynch him after he was convicted of murdering Thomas Wilson. The mob stopped to help put out a fire at the Methodist church, and the jailer escaped with his prisoner in the meantime. Papers from Maryland to Louisiana carried the story of the prisoner saved by a church fire.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jim Harris
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jim Harris took place at Vicksburg, Mississippi, on the night of April 30, 1888, when Harris, a Black man accused of criminally assaulting a woman named Mrs. M. Simmons, was killed the night after the alleged assault. The case reached papers across the country only as a brief wire item, usually paired with the lynching of Henry Pope at Summerville, Georgia, the same night.

episodes.title: Mouse Tail Landing shooting
episodes.lead: The Mouse Tail Landing shooting was the killing of J. Stafford by a man named Ward at Mouse Tail Landing, on the Tennessee River near Paducah, Kentucky, on Saturday, April 21, 1888, after which "a band of lynchers" was reported to be hunting Ward. Ward escaped from the crowd at the landing, and a Louisville dispatch added an unconfirmed rumor that he had been found and shot to death. The dispatch ran in papers from Washington to California, and several Kansas weeklies headlined it as a killing "With a Rumored Lynching."

episodes.title: Beating of "Abbidigal"
episodes.lead: The beating of "Abbidigal" was an attack in May 1888 in Green County, Georgia, in which Black followers of a self-styled "Holy One" pursued him after he left with their money, hanged him to a tree and lashed him until they believed him dead. He was found alive and cared for by white people, and the reports said he could not recover. Newspapers across the country carried the story chiefly because, they said, the "Holy One" was a white man who had stained his skin to pass as Black.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Alberti Rossi
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Alberti Rossi took place on May 18, 1888, at Browntown, a suburb of 'Pittown' (also printed 'Pittson'), Pennsylvania, when a crowd of men and boys hanged an Italian railroad worker from a tree. Rossi, accused of attacking three girls, was lowered alive when some of the men interfered.

episodes.title: Pursuit of Alex Jackson by a lynching party
episodes.lead: The pursuit of Alex Jackson by a lynching party took place at Brooksville, Florida, in May 1888, after Jackson, a Black man, was accused of shooting and killing Lucinda Berry, a Black woman. The lynching party and the sheriff's posse both hunted him, but neither caught him, and he was later captured at Ocala and jailed. The New York Sun presented the manhunt as a 'race' between the lynchers and the sheriff.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of the Corbett brothers
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of the Corbett brothers took place in south Florida in the spring of 1888, when stock owners of De Soto county seized brothers accused of stealing cattle and put ropes around their necks. One brother was lifted off the ground before the cattlemen relented and gave the brothers ten days to leave the country or be hanged. The story ran in papers from Texas to New Hampshire, mostly in the cattlemen's own telling.

episodes.title: Killing of Arthur Harton
episodes.lead: The killing of Arthur Harton took place near Curtis, Arkansas, in May 1888, when five Black men took Harton, a Black man, from his bed and beat him to death with an iron bar in a nearby thicket. Four of the five were arrested, and the papers that carried the story drew attention to the fact that three of the men were preachers. A later news summary said Harton had been accused of immorality.

episodes.title: Reported flaying of a Black man in Craven County, North Carolina (1888)
episodes.lead: The reported flaying of a Black man in Craven County, North Carolina, was a story carried by Southern newspapers in late May and early June 1888 that a man described as 'a negro' had been skinned alive by the friends of a young woman teacher he was accused of assaulting. According to the story he died a few minutes after the flaying, which was done at the teacher's request. The account traced to a single source, J. T. Winfield of Craven County, and the Washington Gazette, which first printed it, called it a rumor whose truth was 'not vouched for.'

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Ben Cunningham
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Ben Cunningham occurred in late May 1888 near Wilkinsville, in Union County, South Carolina, when a party pursued Cunningham, a Black tenant accused of striking a white youth, Gunning Byers, on the head, amid what a wire report called 'much talk of lynching him.' Cunningham was arrested by officers the next day and taken toward the courthouse, and no violence against him was reported. The case drew notice chiefly through a Columbia dispatch that reported Byers murdered, a claim local papers later contradicted.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Charles Smith
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Charles Smith took place in East Liverpool, Ohio, early on May 21, 1888, when about five hundred people surrounded the City Hall where Smith, a Black man accused of assaulting a 12-year-old girl, was held. Officers barred the doors, the crowd dispersed, and Smith was committed to jail the same day.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Ben Cunningham
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Ben Cunningham took place in upper Union County, South Carolina, in late May 1888, when a party pursued Cunningham, a Black tenant farmer accused of killing his landlord's sixteen-year-old son, Gunning Byers, amid 'much talk of lynching him.' Officers arrested Cunningham the next day and took him toward the courthouse, and a local correspondent later reported that Byers had survived. The case drew notice mainly through a Columbia dispatch that predicted Cunningham would never come to trial, an account the same correspondent called 'quite erroneous.'

episodes.title: Lynching of Dan Sale
episodes.lead: The lynching of Dan Sale was the hanging of a Black man by a party of about twenty-five men near the village of Danburg, Wilkes County, Georgia, on the night of Sunday, May 6, 1888. Sale, accused of attempting to assault a white schoolteacher, Miss Sallie Smith, had been bound over by a justice of the peace when he was taken from a bailiff and hanged to a tree by the roadside. The story ran as a short Atlanta wire item from Washington to California, and a Savannah dispatch called it the only lynching ever to occur in Wilkes County.

episodes.title: Lynching of Dandy Hook, Chitwood and two others
episodes.lead: The lynching of Dandy Hook, Chitwood and two others took place on the night of Thursday, May 17, 1888, when a party of vigilantes hanged four men accused of horse stealing in No Man's Land, near Woodward, Indian Territory. Two of the dead were described as known outlaws, while the other two were strangers who protested their innocence to the end. The story ran nationally as a wire item, and one dispatch stated that there was 'no reasonable certainty' that the two strangers were guilty.

episodes.title: Lynching of Dave Southall
