episodes.lead: The lynching of Dave Southall was the killing of a Black man by a large crowd of masked men in Louisiana on the night of Sunday, 13 May 1888, as a deputy sheriff took him through the country after his arrest. Southall had been charged with raising a mob and attempting to kill a man who had challenged his right to vote in Pointe Coupee Parish. A single New Orleans dispatch about the killing ran in at least thirteen papers across the country, under headlines that ranged from 'Lynched in Louisiana' to 'A Case of Poetic Justice'.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of David James
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of David James was a manhunt near Aspen, Colorado, in early May 1888, in which a posse pursued James, accused of assaulting a young neighbor girl, with the declared intention of lynching him if he was caught. No lynching was reported, and a brief notice a few days later said James was in jail.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Ed Chamberlain
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Ed Chamberlain occurred at Monticello, White County, Indiana, on May 26, 1888, when crowds gathered at the jail holding Chamberlain, who had been indicted for the murder of Ida Wittenberg and recaptured after a jailbreak in which Sheriff Henderson was badly beaten. State militia guarded the jail, an armed party approaching the town halted or broke up, and officers later moved Chamberlain secretly to the Michigan City penitentiary. Papers across the country reported a lynching as expected, and Chamberlain later hanged himself in jail at Logansport during his trial in December.

episodes.title: Sandy Ridge posse fight
episodes.lead: The Sandy Ridge posse fight was an armed clash on May 4, 1888, in Lowndes County, Alabama, between a sheriff's posse making arrests and a group of armed Black men. Two or three deputies were wounded, and the governor sent state troops; reports of Black casualties ranged from "several negroes killed" to none hurt. Days later a dispatch said a wounded man, Emerson Shepherd, had died after swearing to a plot to massacre whites.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Frank Shank
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Frank Shank was a written demand, dated at East Germantown, Indiana, on May 28, 1888, that the sheriff of Wayne County surrender Shank to 'Judge Lynch' at midnight on May 29. Shank was then in jail, accused of cutting the throat of Lulu Penny, a young schoolteacher who had rejected him. No report of an attack on the jail appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Lynching of George Martin
episodes.lead: The lynching of George Martin was the killing of a miner by a mob near Warrior, Jefferson County, Alabama, on the night of May 1, 1888, hours after he was accused of shooting the town's acting marshal, Owen Kelly. Officers tried to move Martin to Birmingham in the caboose of a freight train, but a mob stopped the train, took him from his guards, hanged him to a tree and shot his body. The story ran nationally as a wire item, sometimes naming him Morton.

episodes.title: Disappearance of George Washington in posse custody
episodes.lead: The disappearance of George Washington in posse custody took place in Catahoula Parish, Louisiana, in or before early May 1888, when a Black boy accused of killing a white farmer was captured by a constable and posse and never brought to Harrisonburg. Two Louisiana papers supposed that he had been killed on the way, one suggesting a hanging, but neither reported his death as fact.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Gus Harris and Loomis Wilson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Gus Harris and Loomis Wilson was a reported rush on the jail at Vandalia, Michigan, in early May 1888 by a crowd of Black residents seeking two Black men held on suspicion of murdering John Atkens. According to a wire dispatch, the unarmed crowd could not get into the jail, and no one was hurt. The story ran under lynching headlines as far as Washington and Dakota, though fuller regional accounts of the murder do not mention an attack on the jail.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Hicks Carmichael
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Hicks Carmichael took place at Knoxville, Tennessee, on the night of May 24, 1888, when a crowd of about 2,000 men and boys gathered at the jail demanding Carmichael, a Black laborer charged with killing Knox County Deputy Sheriff D. A. Shipe four days earlier. Officers had already removed him, and he spent the night in the jail at Chattanooga. Brought back under armed guard, he was tried and sentenced on May 26 and hanged in the Knoxville jail on July 20. Papers disagreed over whether any lynching had been attempted, and Knoxville dispatches later called the early reports exaggerated.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Max Hoppe
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Max Hoppe took place in late May and early June 1888 in northern Montana Territory, after Hoppe was accused of shooting John Adams at a camp near Fort Conrad and pursuers from that settlement took up his trail. No lynching followed: Hoppe was held by Canadian mounted police, extradited, and sentenced at Fort Benton to twenty years for second-degree murder. The case drew a Great Falls editorial urging that 'the intention to lynch him' be abandoned for the sake of Montana's reputation.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of a Chinese man near Warm Springs, California
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of a Chinese man near Warm Springs, California, took place on the morning of May 25, 1888, when a group of people put a rope around the neck of an unnamed man accused of burglary and lifted him off the ground. The rancher whose house had been robbed got the man away alive and turned him over to a constable. A California Associated Press dispatch carried the story as a "Narrow Escape of a Chinese Thief From Being Lynched."

episodes.title: Lynching of James Hicks
episodes.lead: The lynching of James Hicks was the killing of a Black man by Black neighbors near Port Gibson, Mississippi, reported in early May 1888. Accused of attempting to outrage a 7-year-old girl, Hicks was whipped by the girl's father and then shot and hanged by neighbors who judged the whipping insufficient. The story ran as a brief in distant papers, one headed "Summary Punishment."

episodes.title: Reported lynching of James Massey
episodes.lead: The reported lynching of James Massey refers to the disappearance in May 1888 of a Cheatham County, Tennessee, man arrested on a charge of attempted rape, whom citizens were believed to have lynched while he was being taken to Ashland City. Dispatches from Clarksville first called a lynching probable and then said he had probably been lynched, but no report confirming his death appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Rhea County quadruple lynching
episodes.lead: The Rhea County quadruple lynching was the reported killing by a mob, in May 1888, of four Black men held in the jail at Washington, the seat of Rhea County, Tennessee, after they were accused of assaulting a white woman and her daughter. A Chattanooga dispatch named the four as James Strickland, Nick Webster, Jerry Long and Sam Sibner and predicted that a mob would lynch them; a day later, a Spring City special reported that it had. Every report of the lynching was second-hand, and the coverage contains no local confirmation, inquest or arrests.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Newton
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John Newton took place in May 1888 at the jail in Washington, Beaufort County, North Carolina, where a mob gathered to lynch Newton, a white man accused of complicity in the murder of the lumberman Joshua A. Cox. The jail was strongly guarded and the mob abandoned its plan, and Newton was later tried and convicted as an accessory after the fact. The attempt followed the lynching of Cox's accused killer, Thomas Frazier, a few days earlier.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Smith
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John Smith took place at Waldron, Arkansas, on May 22, 1888, when a crowd took Smith, who was jailed on a charge of arson, from the jail twice and strung him up. Both times he was taken down alive when "cooler counsel prevailed" and was returned to jail. A short wire dispatch carried the story to papers as far off as Delaware, South Carolina, Georgia and Dakota Territory.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Wright
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Wright took place in St. Helena, Napa County, California, early on May 5, 1888, when a mob of masked men took Wright from the town jail and hanged him from a bridge. Wright had been accused of shooting and killing Budd Vann, a young man of the town, about two weeks earlier, and had been brought to St. Helena for his preliminary examination. A coroner's jury blamed unknown persons, and a Napa County grand jury adjourned without indictments after censuring local officials.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Frank Koehler
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Frank Koehler took place in Union City, Pennsylvania, in May 1888, when a crowd tried to take Koehler, a German baker arrested on suspicion of dynamiting the house of attorney F. H. McClintock, from the officer who held him. Koehler was not taken, and about a week later a crowd of some 500 people surrounded him with threats at his hearing in the town. He was never convicted of the bombing, but in December 1888 he was returned to Sing Sing prison in New York, from which he had escaped in 1873.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Laurie Davis
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Laurie Davis took place in late April or early May 1888 near Spencer's Store, Virginia, when friends of W. D. Smith, a Stokes county, North Carolina, tobacco peddler, captured Davis, a Black man accused of shooting Smith. According to the Western Sentinel of Winston-Salem, some of the captors had to be restrained from lynching him, and he was instead jailed at Danbury to await requisition by the Governor of South Carolina.

episodes.title: Lynching of Manuel Bowers
episodes.lead: The lynching of Manuel Bowers was the hanging of a Black man to a tree in his own yard in Louisiana in May 1888, a few days after a posse captured him near Coushatta. Bowers was accused of shooting and killing Chas. Huguely near Indian Village about two weeks earlier. The only account found is a single sentence in a weekly paper's column of state news, which named no one in the hanging party.

episodes.title: Lynching of Morely
episodes.lead: The lynching of Morely was the hanging, in early May 1888, of a man named Morely or Morley, 'said to be a half-breed', at or near Oak Ridge settlement, Mississippi, after he was accused of waylaying and shooting James Newbaker. The only account was a brief wire dispatch from Vicksburg, which said no particulars of the hanging had been learned. Newspapers from Georgia to Kansas reprinted it within about a week.

episodes.title: Osceola murders and threatened lynching (1888)
episodes.lead: The Osceola murders and threatened lynching took place in late May 1888, when a widow and her teenage son were beaten to death in their cabin four miles from Osceola, Mississippi County, Arkansas, and four men held for the crime were threatened with lynching. The wire called her Mrs. Stokes Allen and the Osceola Times called her Mrs. Mary Warren. Papers across the country predicted that the accused, a Black tenant named John King and three white men, would be hanged by a mob, but no lynching was reported.

episodes.title: Killing of Pickens Pendergrass and threatened lynching of Summer Little
episodes.lead: The killing of Pickens Pendergrass and threatened lynching of Summer Little took place near Heflin, Alabama, in May 1888, when Pendergrass, of Davisville, was shot dead and about forty armed citizens searched for Little, a Black man accused of the shooting, intending to lynch him. Alfred Newell, said to be implicated, was jailed at Edwardsville; Little remained at large.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Robert Gibson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Robert Gibson took place at Barnesville, Belmont County, Ohio, on the night of May 24, 1888, when a crowd broke into the town lockup, seized Gibson, a Black man accused of sexually assaulting a five-year-old white girl, and whipped him in a field outside town. After proposals to hang him were voted down, he was returned to the officers alive, although the first wire report said he had been hanged. The case drew further notice when the county grand jury declined to indict Gibson and Barnesville men, including the girl's father, were indicted for the mob's work.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Robert L. McNeill
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Robert L. McNeill was an armed manhunt in Moore County, North Carolina, in May 1888, after McNeill shot Miss Ida Poe at a hotel in Carthage. According to special telegrams from Raleigh, a large party of mounted, armed men searched for him on the night of May 5 and the following days "with the avowed intention of lynching him." McNeill escaped, was reported in South Carolina, and by June was said to have been arrested at Fayetteville and released on bond.

episodes.title: Rochelle shooting and lynching threats (1888)
episodes.lead: The Rochelle shooting and lynching threats took place in Rochelle, Georgia, on a Saturday night in May 1888, when a Black man accused of shooting a Mr. Walker with a shotgun was jailed amid threats to lynch him. Walker suffered only a scalp wound, and no attempt on the jailed man was reported, though the Savannah Morning News wrote that "at one time lynching was feared."

episodes.title: Killing of Stephen Allchin
episodes.lead: The killing of Stephen Allchin was the shooting death of Stephen W. Allchin in front of a store at Hempstead, Waller County, Texas, on May 19, 1888, by Deputy Sheriff Dick Springfield and Jack McDade. Both men were charged with murder and refused bail, and the state sent Texas Rangers to Hempstead to keep order and protect witnesses. Texas papers called the killing an "assassination" and described a "reign of terror" in Waller County.

episodes.title: Lynching of Thomas Frazier
episodes.lead: The lynching of Thomas Frazier was the killing of a white man by masked men at Blount's Creek, in Beaufort County, North Carolina, on the night of May 5–6, 1888. Accused of shooting Joshua Cox, a lumberman who had refused him liquor, Frazier was taken from a guarded temporary prison and shot to death where Cox had fallen. Wire reports carried the story nationally, while North Carolina papers disagreed over whether it was justice or a disgrace.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Tom Collins
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Tom Collins took place in Wichita, Kansas, on the night of May 26, 1888, when a report spread that a mob would storm the county jail and hang Collins, a Black man accused of raping a widow. Sheriff Hays armed guards, a militia company stood ready and a party of Black men gathered to protect the prisoner, and no mob appeared. Collins was later tried twice, convicted and sentenced to nine years in the penitentiary.

episodes.title: Lynching of Tom Roney
episodes.lead: The lynching of Tom Roney was the hanging of a Black farm hand by a mob near Woodburn, in Warren County, Kentucky, in the second week of May 1888. Roney was accused of poisoning the horses of a farmer who had discharged him, and he was taken from the house where he lived and hanged from a tree. A Bowling Green wire report carried the story to papers across the country, and one account called it the first hanging in Warren County in many years.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Alex Umphreys
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Alex Umphreys was an attack on a Black prisoner by his fellow inmates in the county jail at Columbus, Ohio, on May 16, 1888, after he was jailed on a charge of assaulting a young girl. Inmates nearly drowned him and hoisted him from the floor by a rope around his neck, but he survived. A wire dispatch saying that "Judge Lynch" had come close to ending his life ran in papers from Washington to Texas and Kansas over the following ten days.

episodes.title: Lynching of Allen Sturgis
episodes.lead: The lynching of Allen Sturgis took place at Thomson, McDuffie County, Georgia, on the night of June 2-3, 1888, when men broke into the town jail, took Sturgis, a young Black man held on burglary charges, and hanged him from an oak beside a road at the edge of town. A coroner's jury found that he died "by parties to us unknown." Local reports called it the first lynching ever in McDuffie County, and brief wire and digest items carried it across the country.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Amos Miller
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Amos Miller took place in June 1888 at Franklin, Williamson County, Tennessee, when a mob reported at 75 to 100 men went to the county jail to seize Miller, a Black man about 21 years old accused of criminally assaulting Mrs. Scott, a white woman of Maury County. Officers had taken him out ahead of the mob, which searched the jail, failed to find him and dispersed, and he was taken to Nashville for safekeeping. Papers told the story as one of officers outwitting lynchers, but on August 10, 1888, Miller was taken from the Franklin courtroom and hanged by about fifty armed men.

episodes.title: Lynching of Andrew Grandstaff
episodes.lead: The lynching of Andrew Grandstaff took place at Viroqua, Vernon County, Wisconsin, in the early morning of June 2, 1888, when a mob broke into the county jail, took Grandstaff from the sheriff and hanged him from an oak in front of the court house. Grandstaff had been arrested the night before on a charge of murdering Reuben Drake, Drake's wife and their two grandchildren, and officers said he had confessed. The wire story ran from Pennsylvania to Montana, and Wisconsin weeklies divided over it.

episodes.title: Reported threatened lynching of Arthur Burton
episodes.lead: The reported threatened lynching of Arthur Burton followed his arrest at Brownsville, Linn County, Oregon, in June 1888, when Burton, described as "a mulatto," was charged with raping Eliza Harrington, a girl of about sixteen. A condensed regional news column said Burton escaped lynching only through the efforts of his guard, and the story was reprinted in Idaho papers in July. Brownsville's own correspondent called the report of an attempted lynching "without foundation," and no report of the outcome of the case was found.

episodes.title: Killing of Bryson near Dardanelle, Arkansas
episodes.lead: The killing of Bryson near Dardanelle, Arkansas, was the shooting of a man pursued by a posse in June 1888, whose body was found in the Arkansas River a few miles below Dardanelle on Sunday, June 10. He had been accused of attempting to assault the wife of a man named Shinn, and a dispatch from Little Rock said Shinn had raised the posse that caught him. The story ran as a brief wire item in papers from Indiana to Nebraska.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Charles Blackman
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Charles Blackman refers to a manhunt in Schley County, Georgia, in June 1888, after Blackman, a Black man under sentence of death for the murder of Stonewall Tondee, escaped from the jail at Americus. A Macon dispatch printed in Richmond said large bodies of men had organized to hunt him and predicted a lynching if bloodhounds found him. No lynching followed: a Stewart County deputy sheriff captured Blackman in mid-June, and a court resentenced him to hang that fall.

episodes.title: Killing of Charles Gross
episodes.lead: The killing of Charles Gross was the whipping to death of a farmer in Pulaski County, Missouri, by a band of masked night riders on the night of June 23, 1888. The cause assigned in the dispatches was that Gross had revealed the secrets of the Agricultural Wheel, a secret organization. Papers across the country ran the story as an outrage by a band likened to the White Caps of Indiana, and one dispatch reported arrests, but no later account of a prosecution was found.

episodes.title: Lynching of Robert Robertson
episodes.lead: The lynching of Robert Robertson was the hanging of a Black private of the Twenty-fifth Infantry by masked men at Sun River, Montana Territory, about midnight on June 10–11, 1888. Robertson, called Robinson in many reports, was accused of fatally shooting Charles McGuire, a Sun River freighter, and was taken from a deputy at the Sun River jail. A judge sitting at Great Falls charged the grand jury against the lynchers, whom the grand jury could not identify.

episodes.title: Lynching of Chubb McCarthy
episodes.lead: The lynching of Chubb McCarthy took place early on 28 June 1888, when a mob took McCarthy, accused of murdering Mike Dorsey, from the jail at Minneapolis, Kansas, and hanged him from a bridge over the Solomon River. The mob held the sheriff and city marshal under guard while it worked, and the body was found hanging at 7 a.m. Newspapers across the country reported it as the last of four lynchings in Kansas within twenty-four hours, which the wire report linked to the state's death-penalty law.

episodes.title: Lynching of Dennis Williams
episodes.lead: The lynching of Dennis Williams took place at Ellaville, Florida, in June 1888, when a mob took Williams, a Black man accused of shooting a mill superintendent, from the men guarding him and killed him. His body was found in the Suwanee River riddled with bullets. The story ran in papers across the country as a short Tallahassee dispatch, which added that Black residents were reported to be planning revenge.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Doc Carnegie
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Doc Carnegie was a reported plan in late June 1888 by a mob of Black residents of Birmingham, Alabama, to take Carnegie, a Black man jailed on a charge of murdering his wife, from the jail and lynch him. Police and deputy sheriffs were put on guard at the jail, and no report of an attack or of Carnegie's fate was found. The Memphis Appeal reported the plot under the headline "Negro Lynchers Organizing," stressing that the would-be lynchers were said to be of the accused man's own race.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Thomas Hourigan
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Thomas Hourigan was an armed mob's attack on the jail at Lebanon, Kentucky, on the night of Tuesday, June 26, 1888, aimed at hanging a physician held for killing his brother-in-law. The mob battered down his cell door but scattered when an officer fired a pistol into it, and Hourigan escaped unhurt. Kentucky papers and a Louisville wire dispatch treated it as a narrow escape, which one headline called "A Close Call From a Mob."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching at Duluth, Georgia (1888)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching at Duluth, Georgia, was a failed effort in June 1888 by citizens in and near Duluth to take an unnamed Black man from officers and lynch him after he was accused of attempting to rape a girl of about ten. After a crowd of 100 was reported to be coming for him at Lawrenceville, the sheriff obtained a judge's order and moved him to the jail at Monroe. Georgia papers carried the episode as a brief state-news item.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of E. Langley Jones
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of E. Langley Jones was an incident at Colorado City, Texas, in which a Scurry county posse hunting horse thieves seized Jones, a rancher, and prepared to hang him. He was freed when an Englishman in the posse and the Sheriff proved he had been mistaken for another man. The only known account is Jones's own signed narrative, printed without a date for the incident in the Los Angeles Daily Herald on June 10, 1888.

episodes.title: Killing of an unnamed Black man in Madison Parish, Louisiana (1888)
episodes.lead: The killing of an unnamed Black man in Madison Parish, Louisiana, took place in or before June 1888, after a resident named T. H. Iler captured him on an accusation of robbery. Iler was charged with the killing and acquitted after a trial in Vicksburg, having claimed that two unknown men lynched the man.

episodes.title: Goodlettsville manhunt of 1888
episodes.lead: The Goodlettsville manhunt of 1888 was a search near Goodlettsville, Tennessee, in late June 1888 by a posse or mob for an unnamed Black man accused of raping and knifing a young woman engaged to be married. Nashville dispatches said he would be lynched if caught, but no report of his capture appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Lynching of Frank Davis
episodes.lead: The lynching of Frank Davis was the hanging of a Black man by masked men in the court-house yard at Tupelo, Mississippi, early on June 19, 1888. Davis, charged with an attempted rape of a girl at Saltillo, was taken from the Lee County jail after the lynchers seized Sheriff Long. Memphis and Mississippi papers carried the story under the headline "A Negro Rapist Lynched," and later counted it among three lynchings in the state in one week.

episodes.title: Lynching of Frank Lang'y
episodes.lead: The lynching of Frank Lang'y was the hanging, in Oklahoma in about May or June 1888, of a man described as an outlaw, after local people took him from the officers who held him. It is known from a single brief in the Turner County Herald of Hurley, Dakota, which gave no date beyond 'recently' and no place more exact than Oklahoma.

episodes.title: Lynching of Schenck (Monarch, Colorado)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Schenck was the hanging of a one-legged gambler by a mob at Monarch, Colorado, on the night of June 13, 1888, after he was accused of shooting two men in a saloon row. The mob hanged him to a telegraph pole, and the dispatch reported that friends of the dead men were gathering and that more trouble was feared. The story reached papers across the country as one short wire item from Salida and was then condensed into weekly news digests.

episodes.title: Lynching of an unnamed Black man at Grand Forks, Dakota
episodes.lead: The lynching of an unnamed Black man at Grand Forks, Dakota, was a mob killing reported only in a June 1888 editorial in the Western Appeal of St. Paul, Minnesota, which dated it to "only a short time ago." According to the editorial, the man was accused of raping a white woman, pursued into Minnesota by a mob, taken back to Grand Forks and torn apart by teams of horses. The paper cited the case as proof that lynching for alleged rape reached "even up here, in the free Northwest," and said the woman later admitted he had not raped her.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Grant Alexander
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Grant Alexander took place in June 1888, when a Black man jailed on a charge of assaulting a white woman in Boughton township was the target of several failed attempts to lynch him. Black residents guarded the jail each night to protect him, and the local paper criticized the sheriffs for relying on a guard of Black men while also opposing lynch law.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Grant Holly
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Grant Holly took place in Nevada County, Arkansas, in about June 1888, when armed men and gathered citizens tried to seize a Black man accused of attempting to assault a white woman near Bowden. The sheriff moved Holly to the state penitentiary at Little Rock for safe-keeping, and in November a deputy took him back to Prescott for trial.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Foster
episodes.lead: The lynching of Henry Foster was the hanging of a Black hired man by members of a citizen pursuing party near Lansing Switch, six miles east of Longview, Texas, on the night of June 7, 1888. Foster had been accused of attempting to assault an elderly white woman near Friendship three days earlier, and the white Texas press reported his death as deserved punishment.

episodes.title: Lynching of James Foster
episodes.lead: The lynching of James Foster was the hanging of a Black man, James Foster, by a mounted mob that took him from the jail at Henderson, Kentucky, late on the night of Sunday, June 10, 1888. Foster had been arrested three days earlier on a charge of criminally assaulting the eight-year-old daughter of John Howard, and the mob hanged him from a tree outside the town. The story ran widely as an Evansville wire; a Henderson correspondent added that part of the mob were Black men and that it nearly lynched a second prisoner.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Jed Pritchett
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Jed Pritchett followed a June 1888 accusation that Pritchett, a Black man, had assaulted an eight-year-old white girl near Danville in Pittsylvania County, Virginia. Armed men and officers searched for him while Virginia papers predicted, and in some cases openly hoped, that he would be lynched when caught. He was arrested in North Carolina in December, and the sheriff moved him to Lynchburg for fear of an attack on the jail.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of John B. Hunter
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of John B. Hunter took place in Culbertson, Nebraska, in June 1888, when a crowd gathered to lynch Hunter, a hardware merchant held for the shooting death of farmer Harry B. Hull. According to the Omaha Bee, about 200 people besieged the sheriff's residence where he was held, but no attack followed, and Hunter was taken to Lincoln for safe keeping. He was tried at Culbertson in December and given a twelve-month sentence, which one dispatch called light.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Bowen
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John Bowen took place early on June 15, 1888, at Union Bridge, Carroll County, Maryland, when a group of men took Bowen, a Black man accused of a razor attack on two Black residents, from the town lockup and tried to hang him. He escaped, was recaptured in Pennsylvania eight days later, and was convicted of assault with intent to kill in December. The first dispatch wrongly reported him lynched, and most papers described the would-be lynchers as Black men, which Bowen disputed.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Bowen
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John Bowen took place at Union Bridge, Carroll County, Maryland, early on June 15, 1888, when a party took Bowen, a Black man held for cutting two Black people with a razor, from the town lockup and tried to hang him. Bowen slipped the noose, was recaptured about a week later and was convicted of assault with intent to kill in December. Wire reports noted that the lynchers were Black men, though Bowen later said most of the crowd was white.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Cowan
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John Cowan was an interrupted hanging at the Post Percheron horse ranch near Cheyenne, Wyoming, reported in a dispatch dated June 27, 1888. Cowan, a cowboy accused by his fellow workmen of rifling a trunk, was tried and sentenced to hang by the ranch's cowboys and had a rope around his neck when the foreman intervened. Cowan survived and was ordered off the ranch.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Andrew Johnson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John Andrew Johnson refers to repeated mob threats in June and October 1888 against Johnson, a nineteen-year-old Black man held at Crockett, Houston County, Texas, on a charge of raping a white girl. Officers moved him to Houston and later guarded the Crockett jail to keep him from the crowds, and he was legally hanged on December 21, 1888, after a conviction in the district court. Texas papers followed the threats as near misses, and the execution ran as a wire item across the country.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of John Studebaker
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of John Studebaker was a week-long mob threat in June 1888 against a farmer jailed at Jetmore, Hodgeman County, Kansas, for the shooting of his neighbor Thomas Andrews. A mob of more than 100 men was expected nightly, but the sheriff and armed townspeople guarded the jail, and no attack is reported.

episodes.title: Killing of Joshua Anderson
episodes.lead: The killing of Joshua Anderson was the fatal stabbing of a farmer near Owensboro, Kentucky, in late spring 1888 by one of four men who had disguised themselves as "White Caps" to whip him. The men were said to have whipped Anderson once and ordered him to leave, then killed him when they tried to whip him a second time; the principals were arrested.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Stewart
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of William Stewart took place near Lafayette, a village north of London, Ohio, in early June 1888, when townspeople threatened to lynch a Black man accused of assaulting a white woman. Stewart had been caught and jailed, and no attack on him is reported. The episode is known from two items in the Springfield daily republic of June 4, 1888.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching at Manly, North Carolina (1888)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching at Manly, North Carolina, was a manhunt on June 29, 1888, in which a large party of mounted white men searched for an unnamed Black man accused of assaulting a white woman, intending to lynch him. The only report found, a Raleigh telegram to the Richmond Dispatch, does not say whether the man was caught or what became of him.

episodes.title: Lynching of Ned Clark
episodes.lead: The lynching of Ned Clark was the shooting of a Black man, described in the press as "colored," by the men holding him prisoner in Worth County, Georgia, reported on June 26, 1888. Clark had been charged with attempting to assault a thirteen-year-old girl, and his captors said he was shot while trying to escape as they took him toward Irwin County; his body was found with nineteen bullets in it. The account, which came from a single dispatch out of Albany, ran in papers across the country and put Clark's name on a year-end list of the "Victims of Judge Lynch."

episodes.title: Death of an accused poisoner at Windsor, Missouri
episodes.lead: The death of an accused poisoner at Windsor, Missouri, took place on June 3, 1888, when a Black servant girl in the household of a Windsor man named Owsley died after drinking coffee she was accused of poisoning. A widely reprinted wire dispatch said she had been forced to drink the coffee and died within half an hour, while two Missouri dispatches said she tasted it at her mistress's word or drank it when accused of being afraid.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Sam Haines
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Sam Haines was a manhunt in June 1888 at a place printed as 'Rochville' or 'Rochvine', reported from Atlanta, Georgia, after Haines, a Black man, was accused of killing his wife and their two-day-old child. A search party of both white and Black men pursued him, and the dispatch said he would be lynched when found. No report of his capture or of a lynching appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Shooting and disappearance of a Black man near Sycamore, Georgia
episodes.lead: The shooting and disappearance of a Black man near Sycamore, Georgia, took place in June 1888, after J. F. Horkan shot an unnamed "negro man" accused of making "insulting proposals" to a white girl in his household. Neighbors threatened to lynch the wounded man, but Horkan refused; days later the man vanished, and it was "generally supposed he was lynched."

episodes.title: Lynching of Wallace Mitchell
episodes.lead: The lynching of Wallace Mitchell took place at Syracuse, Hamilton County, Kansas, early on June 27, 1888, when a crowd of a hundred or more men took him from jail and hanged him for the murder of a twelve-year-old boy, Oscar Johnson. The men got in after the sheriff fled with the keys and hanged Mitchell from a telegraph pole where the killing had occurred. Many papers reported it as one of four Kansas lynchings in twenty-four hours.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Charles Washington
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Charles Washington took place near Florence, Howard County, Maryland, in late June 1888, when a Black boy of about ten, accused of cutting the throats of two young white children in his care, was met with threats of lynching after his arrest. No mob formed against him; he was jailed at Ellicott City, tried for murder in September, and acquitted. Papers treated the case as notable chiefly for the age of the accused, whose youth one telegram gave as the reason he was unlikely to suffer mob violence.

episodes.title: Lynching of Washington Ives
episodes.lead: The lynching of Washington Ives was the hanging of a Black man near Natchez, Mississippi, on the night of June 16, 1888, after he was accused of attempting to assault a young woman. His body was found the next morning hanging from a tree with a card warning against rape, and no one was reported arrested. The Natchez wire report ran in papers from New York to Georgia, and the case later appeared on a year-end list of the "Victims of Judge Lynch."

episodes.title: Lynching of William Moore
episodes.lead: The lynching of William Moore took place early on June 26, 1888, when a mob of armed men broke into the jail at Charleston, Coles County, Illinois, and hanged Moore, a Black man from Mattoon, from the water tank near the depot. He had been accused of assaulting a young white woman, Mary A. Bumgardner, and was being held for the grand jury. Within days, dispatches from her home district called her of bad repute and Moore innocent, and in October nine men were indicted.

episodes.title: Plot to lynch William Patterson
episodes.lead: The plot to lynch William Patterson was a plan by fewer than a dozen citizens of Louisville, Kentucky, to take Patterson, a Black man under sentence of death, from the jail and hang him if Governor Buckner pardoned him. The plan was made public on June 17, 1888, after the governor announced he would not interfere, and Patterson was legally hanged five days later.

episodes.title: Lynching of William Stokes
episodes.lead: The lynching of William Stokes was the killing of a Black farm laborer who was shot dead after being taken from a constable's custody near Marmora, Dinwiddie County, Virginia, in June 1888. Stokes had been arrested on a charge arising from alleged entries into houses on the farm where he had worked, and his body was found in a road a short distance from where he had been held. A coroner's jury found that he had been shot by persons unknown, and in August a Dinwiddie grand jury dismissed the matter for lack of evidence. Virginia papers treated the case as a lynching carried out with such secrecy that no one was ever suspected.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Woods
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of William Woods took place in Sherman, Texas, in June 1888, when a crowd threatened to lynch Woods, a young Black man jailed on a charge of assaulting Mrs. Maggie Miles, a white servant. Officers brought him into the jail under guard, and reports of a likely alibi led the crowd to hold back. One Austin paper nevertheless headlined that he had been "Strung Up to a Tree," a claim its own text did not support.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Patrick
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of William Patrick was a series of reported mob threats in Indiana in 1888 against a man jailed for the killing of a bartender named Carter at Spencer. A June dispatch from Evansville said Patrick, held at Rockport, was in hourly danger of being lynched by his victim's kin, who had already dug his grave. No attack took place, and in October Patrick was sentenced to two years in the penitentiary.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Risbee and Wyley Lee
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Risbee and Wyley Lee took place at Chetopa, Kansas, in the early morning of June 27, 1888, when a mob of 200 to 300 men took the two Black men from a sheriff's guard and hanged them from a newspaper office window. The two had been accused of shooting the town marshal and his deputy, both of whom were later reported alive. Papers noted it chiefly for a coroner's jury of four white and eight Black men that split over naming the mob.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of A. N. Willey
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of A. N. Willey took place at Sunset, Texas, in June 1888, after the physician was accused of stripping and whipping his wife and chasing her through the street with a pistol. Citizens disarmed and held him, and deputy sheriffs took him to the county jail at Montague; dispatches from Gainesville said he was moved "to prevent lynching by the infuriated citizens." The wire story ran nationally; one Ohio paper printed that he was "now being lynched," and several headlines faulted the town for not lynching him.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Humphreys
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Humphreys took place at Asheville, North Carolina, in the early morning of 15 July 1888, when a band of twenty-five to forty masked men broke into the county jail, took out the Black prisoner and hanged him to a tree. Humphreys had been arrested the night before, accused of assaulting a thirteen-year-old white girl, and was hanged before any trial. The Charlotte Democrat called it the first lynching known in Western North Carolina, and the Asheville dispatch was reprinted across the country.

episodes.title: Killing of Barfield in Miller County, Georgia
episodes.lead: The killing of Barfield took place in Miller County, Georgia, shortly before July 2, 1888; the papers gave neither his first name nor his race. His widow, Elizabeth Barfield, wrote to a federal deputy marshal that he had been "murdered by the kuklux," while another report said a deputy sheriff had killed him as he resisted arrest.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Bill Anderson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Bill Anderson was a threat by a mob at Tuskegee, Alabama, in July 1888 to lynch a 22-year-old Black prisoner held in the Macon County jail. Sheriff Pinkard took Anderson by train to the Montgomery jail before the mob acted, and the story circulated as a wire dispatch in papers from Atlanta to Kansas.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bruce Younger
episodes.lead: The lynching of Bruce Younger took place about midnight on July 26, 1888, at Halifax Court-House, Virginia, when a party of armed horsemen took Younger, a Black man, from the county jail and hanged him from a footbridge. Younger had been arrested that morning, accused of assaulting Mrs. Robert Dodd, a white woman near Meadsville. Virginia papers described it as the first lynching ever carried out in Halifax County, and correspondents there defended it as justified.

episodes.title: Lynching of Calvin Moody
episodes.lead: The lynching of Calvin Moody was the hanging of a Black man accused of murdering his wife, carried out by a mob of about 200 Black men at Moulton, Lawrence County, Alabama, on the night of July 1, 1888, by most accounts. The mob overpowered the sheriff and a guard, took Moody from the jail, and hanged him from a tree outside town after he reportedly confessed. Wire reports printed across the country called it the first lynching in Alabama of a Black man by members of his own race.

episodes.title: Crittenden County lynching rumors of July 1888
episodes.lead: The Crittenden County lynching rumors of July 1888 were two reports that a Black official had been lynched near Marion, Arkansas, during the expulsion of Black county officers from Crittenden County. The first, that legislator Sandy Odom had been hanged, was denied the next day, and the second, a wire dispatch that a Black county official had been hanged by a white mob at Marion, was called unfounded in Memphis. The wire version nonetheless ran in papers from Savannah to Montana, some of them under approving headlines.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Miller and Clarke
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Miller and Clarke was a failed attempt by a mob on the night of Tuesday, July 17, 1888, to take two white men held on rape charges from the jail in Knoxville, Tennessee, and lynch them. Officers at the jail stopped the attempt, and five men, among them a newspaper editor and a reporter, were arrested as members of the mob.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bruce Younger
episodes.lead: The lynching of Bruce Younger was the killing of a Black man by a party of armed horsemen who took him from the jail at Halifax Court House, Virginia, around midnight on July 26–27, 1888, and hanged and shot him at a nearby footbridge. Younger had been arrested the day before, accused of assaulting Mrs. Robert Dodd, the wife of the farmer near Meadsville for whom he worked. The story went out on the wire under a Danville dateline, and some news digests placed the lynching at Danville itself.

episodes.title: Lynching of Dr. G. H. Thomas
episodes.lead: The lynching of Dr. G. H. Thomas was the killing by a mob of a man who called himself Dr. G. H. Thomas, near Oxford, Mississippi, in the early hours of July 17, 1888, after he had been arrested and placed under guard at the farm where he boarded. He was accused of drugging and "ruining" Amelia Shives, his host's daughter, whom he had treated as a physician. Wire reports told the story as the lynching of "a Rapist," but a meeting of citizens east of Oxford condemned the killing as done "without cause or provocation" and called for an investigation.

episodes.title: Lynching of Eli Bryant
episodes.lead: The lynching of Eli Bryant was the hanging of a Black man by a white mob at Harges Station, near Starkville, Mississippi, on July 27, 1888. Bryant had been accused of assaulting a white woman, and papers reported that a crowd of 500 to 800 men hanged him after he was caught. The story went out by wire and ran in Southern, Northern and Mississippi papers over the next three weeks, usually presenting his guilt as settled.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of horse thieves in the Cimarron district (1888)
episodes.lead: The reported lynching of horse thieves in the Cimarron district was an unconfirmed report, carried in a wire dispatch from Clayton, New Mexico, dated July 5, 1888, that settlers had lynched thirteen horse thieves on the night of Monday, July 2. The dispatch itself said the men who brought the report "could give nothing definite," and no confirmation, names or follow-up appear in the coverage. Papers in Dakota and Minnesota nonetheless ran it under headlines stating that settlers had "strung up" eleven horse thieves.

episodes.title: Lynching of Fremont Emmons
episodes.lead: The lynching of Fremont Emmons took place at Pawnee City, Nebraska, in the early hours of July 31, 1888, when a mob took Emmons from deputies guarding him in the court house and hanged him from a railroad bridge. Emmons, a hotel cook, was charged with stabbing to death Bertha Schultz, who worked at the same hotel, after she refused to marry him. A coroner's jury blamed persons unknown, and Nebraska papers called this lynching justified while warning against mobs in general.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Gust Johnson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Gust Johnson took place near Phillips, Wisconsin, on July 12, 1888, when a crowd of railroad section hands and citizens put a rope around the neck of Johnson, a homesteader accused of chaining and flogging his young son. Johnson was released alive after promising never to whip the boy again, but only after the crowd flogged him and ducked him in a railway water tank. Newspapers that carried the story treated the crowd's action as deserved punishment of a "cruel and unnatural father."

episodes.title: Lynching of Hamilton Staples
episodes.lead: The lynching of Hamilton Staples was the killing of a Black man near Atlanta, Texas, reported as having taken place on July 11, 1888. According to a syndicated news digest, Staples was lynched after being accused of assaulting the seventeen-year-old daughter of Hardy McCoy, described as a wealthy planter. The episode is known only from that one sentence, which several Midwestern weeklies printed in the following days.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Ira Waters
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Ira Waters took place at Spartanburg, South Carolina, on July 30, 1888, when a party of white men came to take Waters, a Black prisoner, from the jail and lynch him. A deputy sheriff secretly removed him and delivered him to Columbia for safe keeping. Papers told the story chiefly as an account of the deputy's escape with his prisoner.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jack Walker
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jack Walker was the killing of a Black man at or near Brenham, Texas, on July 23, 1888. A wire report said he was lynched because he struck the wife of a German in a quarrel over a horse, and a Texas paper reported that several German citizens had been arrested as participants. Outside Texas the episode reached readers as a single line in weekly news digests printed in Wisconsin, Dakota and Chicago.

episodes.title: Lynching of James Hagley
episodes.lead: The lynching of James Hagley was the shooting death of a Black man at Alma, Arkansas, on the night of July 2-3, 1888, after he was taken from the town jail at midnight. He had been held on an accusation of attempting to assault a 12-year-old girl, and according to a wire dispatch he was tied to a tree and "slowly shot to pieces." The killing reached distant newspapers only as a one-sentence telegraphic item.

episodes.title: Killing of Jesse Bishop
episodes.lead: The killing of Jesse Bishop was the fatal shooting of a Black man by W. T. Russell, a Chattanooga, Tennessee, policeman, in July 1888. Russell was held for murder and then released on $5,000 bail after a habeas corpus hearing. The case drew renewed notice in late August, when the police chief received an anonymous death threat against Russell.

episodes.title: Killing of Jim Torney
episodes.lead: The killing of Jim Torney was the reported killing of a Black farm laborer by a crowd of white men near Pell City, Alabama, in July 1888, after he eloped with Maude Broyles, the sixteen-year-old white daughter of his employer. Birmingham dispatches said the pursuers recovered the girl and were believed to have killed Torney and thrown his body into the Coosa River, though no report said a body was found. The story broke the same week as the lynching of Frank Stone at Pell City, and a national news digest joined the two cases in a single sentence.

episodes.title: Shooting of John Grayson
episodes.lead: The shooting of John Grayson took place in Abingdon, Virginia, on the evening of Saturday, July 21, 1888, when Grayson, who had just shot a local man named Lilburn Trigg, was hit by a pistol ball fired by an unidentified person as a crowd chased him. Grayson died the next morning, Trigg three days later, and Trigg's mother of shock that night, and newspapers called it a triple tragedy. The Richmond Dispatch's Abingdon correspondent wrote that Grayson would have been lynched had he survived.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Humphreys
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Humphreys was the killing of a Black man by masked men who broke into the county jail at Asheville, North Carolina, early on Sunday, July 15, 1888, and hanged him from a tree. Humphreys had been arrested the night before, accused of assaulting a thirteen-year-old white girl, and the mob spent about an hour battering apart the steel cage that held him. The story ran by wire across the country, and the Charlotte Democrat called it "the first lynching known in Western North Carolina."

episodes.title: Lynching of John Lynn
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Lynn was the killing of a Black man by a mob of thirty-five armed white men at his home in Assumption Parish, Louisiana, in late July 1888. Lynn shot dead one of the attackers before he was captured, and the mob later shot him in twelve places. A New Orleans telegram presented it as one of a series of 'outrages against the blacks' that had prompted talk of an exodus.

episodes.title: Lynching of L. S. Elmer
episodes.lead: The lynching of L. S. Elmer took place early on July 27, 1888, at Wahpeton, Dakota Territory, when a masked mob took the deputy sheriff from the Richland County jail and hanged him from the bridge over the Bois des Sioux River. Elmer was accused of having shot Mollie Korbel, a domestic in the sheriff's household, two days earlier. A coroner's jury blamed persons unknown; the local paper hailed the hanging as justice, and wire reports spread it nationally, stressing that the sheriff would not fire on the mob.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Leander Huff
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Leander Huff took place on July 28, 1888, at Concordia Landing, Mississippi, after Huff, mate of the steamer Coahoma, shot and killed a Black roustabout and a crowd of Black men demanded that he be handed over to be hanged. Huff fled across the river pursued by men in skiffs and turned up alive in Memphis on August 3. Papers retold his flight as "A Race for Life"; he was arrested in Memphis as a fugitive from justice in December.

episodes.title: Killing of Levi Lally
episodes.lead: The killing of Levi Lally was the fatal shooting of a farmer at his house near Montevallo, Alabama, on the night of Saturday, July 21, 1888, by two white men and a Black man who had called him outside. Lally died the next day, and warrants were issued on suspicion against men with whom he had quarrelled over work. The case reached distant papers through a single Montgomery dispatch, and a moonshiner killing in Bibb County, reported about ten days later, bore some resemblance to it.

episodes.title: Killing of Lewis C. Lane
episodes.lead: The killing of Lewis C. Lane took place near Quitman, Georgia, on July 16, 1888, when W. T. Arrington overtook a sheriff who was moving Lane, a Savannah traveling salesman charged with assaulting Arrington's daughter, to the Thomasville jail and shot him dead. Arrington and his brother-in-law Henry T. Williams were later charged with murder and released on bail, and no report of a trial was found. The Savannah Morning News covered the case at length because Lane was well known there, and a letter in its columns called the killing lynch law.

episodes.title: Killing of Mack Henry
episodes.lead: The killing of Mack Henry was the fatal shooting of a Black man by an unknown assailant near Ichetuchnee, Florida, on Friday, July 27, 1888. The only known report, from the Lake City correspondent of the Savannah Morning News, noted that Henry's wife had been shot and killed at the same place about three months earlier.

episodes.title: Reported lynching at Marion, Arkansas
episodes.lead: The reported lynching at Marion, Arkansas, was a wire story of July 24, 1888, that a mob of white men had hanged one of the expelled Black county officials of Crittenden County at Marion the night before. A Memphis dispatch called the report unfounded the same day, and the Memphis Appeal, the governor and the county sheriff had no confirmation of it. The story nonetheless ran in papers across the country, some under headlines such as 'Reports Confirmed', and the Cleveland Gazette treated it as fact.

episodes.title: Torture of a Chinese man near Marysville, California
episodes.lead: The torture of a Chinese man near Marysville, California, took place in late July 1888, when a group of Chinese men at a garden across the Yuba River held a countryman suspended by a rope for three days as an accused thief. After a white man intervened, the captors promised to hand him to the authorities, but he was not seen again, and officers opened an investigation. A California Associated Press dispatch called it "shockingly barbarous treatment," and a Honolulu paper later reprinted it as "Chinese Lynch Law."

episodes.title: Lynching of Morgan Williams
episodes.lead: The lynching of Morgan Williams was the killing of a Black man by a group of Black men in Canton, Mississippi, in late July 1888. According to the only report found, Williams, a stranger in the town, had killed a man named Morgan Jones while defending himself against Jones's attacks. The report named the lynchers only as "negroes" and treated the episode as one item among the week's state news.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of N. F. Anderson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of N. F. Anderson took place on a Friday night in July 1888 at Vermillion, Dakota Territory, when 'enraged neighbors' tried to lynch the local harnessmaker. Anderson, who was said to be a wife-beater, escaped on foot, and the episode appeared only as a one-sentence item in regional news columns.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Gaetano Gamardelli and Napoleon Ems at Rye
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Gaetano Gamardelli and Napoleon Ems took place at Rye, New York, on July 16, 1888, when about 300 armed Italian laborers marched on a justice's office and demanded two arrested men so that they might lynch them. A constable and armed citizens of Rye kept the crowd back and took the prisoners to White Plains prison, and the New York Tribune headlined the story "Saved From Being Lynched."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of R. O. Higgins
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of R. O. Higgins took place in Yancey County, North Carolina, in late July 1888, when a lynching party pursued Higgins, a Black man accused of assaulting a ten-year-old Black girl. No report of Higgins's capture or fate appears in the coverage, which consisted of two brief items in out-of-state papers.

episodes.title: Reported lynching at Roanoke, Virginia (July 1888)
episodes.lead: The reported lynching at Roanoke, Virginia, was the killing of an unnamed Black man, described as "a colored man," said in a single newspaper brief to have been lynched at Roanoke in July 1888. The brief stated that he had confessed to murdering two women, and it gave no other details of the victim, the lynchers or the killing.

episodes.title: Lynching of Robert Bryan
episodes.lead: The lynching of Robert Bryan took place on the evening of July 6, 1888, on the outskirts of Henderson, Kentucky, when about fifty masked men took the Black youth of about sixteen from the men conveying him to jail and hanged him to a tree. Bryan had been accused of stabbing to death Riley Hancock, a nineteen-year-old white man, near Smith's Mills earlier that day. A Nashville American dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, and the Hopkinsville South Kentuckian treated it as the latest in a run of mob actions at Henderson.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Rube Jones
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Rube Jones took place at Fayetteville, Georgia, in July 1888, when a body of armed men broke into the town jail to lynch Jones, an 18-year-old Black prisoner accused of assault with intent to rape. Jones, who was not chained, ran through the crowd at the jail entrance and escaped under pistol fire, reportedly wounded. An Atlanta wire carried the story of his escape to papers from Pennsylvania to Minnesota.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Sampson Dey
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Sampson Dey took place in Norfolk County, Virginia, in the late summer of 1888, after Dey, a Black tenant farmer, was arrested on suspicion of burning the barn of his landlord, George A. Wilson, at Green Ridge. Amid serious threats of lynching, the private detectives who had arrested him removed him to the Portsmouth jail, and he was bound over for trial.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of L. W. Davis at Winslow
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of L. W. Davis took place at Winslow, Arizona Territory, on July 4, 1888, when railroad firemen and engineers tried to hang the roundhouse night watchman for fatally shooting a fireman. The men put a rope around his neck but dispersed after two engineers urged them to let the law take its course, and Davis was jailed at St. Johns on a murder charge. The story spread as a one-line wire item noting that the "murderer narrowly escaped lynching by a mob."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Steve Allen
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Steve Allen took place on the night of Monday, July 2, 1888, when a crowd gathered at the jail in Oxford, Mississippi, to lynch Allen, a Black railroad hand accused of killing his section boss, Hodnett. The sheriff had already moved Allen, and later in July a Holly Springs paper said people were still "determined to lynch this murderer wherever they can find him."

episodes.title: Lynching of William Henry Smith
episodes.lead: The lynching of William Henry Smith took place at Wytheville, Virginia, on the night of July 10, 1888, when a mob took the Black man from a sheriff's guard on a train, hanged him on a hill near the depot and shot his body. Smith had been accused of assaulting an elderly white woman near New River Bridge in Pulaski County the week before. Early wire reports said he had already been hanged near the scene, and Virginia papers printed conflicting versions before the Wytheville account appeared.

episodes.title: Lynching of William Henry Smith
episodes.lead: The lynching of William Henry Smith was the hanging and shooting of a Black man accused of assaulting a white woman in Pulaski County, Virginia, by masked men who took him from the sheriff of Wythe County at the Wytheville depot around midnight in July 1888. Smith, whom other reports called Henry Smith or William Jones, was hanged near the depot and his body riddled with bullets. A wire from Wytheville carried the story nationally, several papers under headlines that endorsed the killing.

episodes.title: Lynching of W. H. Handley
episodes.lead: The lynching of W. H. Handley took place on the night of July 31, 1888, when a mob of about fifty armed men broke into the jail at Carthage, Smith County, Tennessee, took out Handley, and hanged him to a tree. Handley, about 23, was awaiting trial, set for the next day, on a charge of killing a deputy sheriff the previous September. The papers noted the resistance of the sheriff and his posse, who exchanged about thirty shots with the mob before it reached the prisoner.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Wash Attaway
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Wash Attaway took place at the jail in Sulphur Springs, Texas, in July 1888, when a mob demanded Attaway, a Black man held for the killing of a white man named Marion Gamblin near Carroll's Prairie. The mob, put at ninety-five men, was kept at bay, and Attaway was later reported released on bail. Texas papers noted the case for its toll: besides Gamblin, two women's deaths were attributed to the affair.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Bailey
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of William Bailey took place at Morris, Illinois, in July 1888, when a sheriff was reported to be having trouble preventing the lynching of Bailey, a Black man accused of assaulting a thirteen-year-old girl. The episode is known only from a single sentence carried in newspaper roundups, and no report of its outcome was found.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of William Smith at Penryn Park
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of William Smith took place at Penryn Park, Pennsylvania, on the evening of July 13, 1888, when a crowd threatened to hang the older White Oak man just after his arrest on a charge of abducting five-year-old Bertha Beck. A man produced a rope and another struck Smith, but he was taken under guard to the jail at Lebanon. The Lancaster Intelligencer, which had called him a villain, soon rebuked the 'hotheads', and a Lebanon court acquitted Smith of the abduction in September.

episodes.title: Bayou Martin raid
episodes.lead: The Bayou Martin raid was an armed attack in August 1888 in which about 250 white men surprised Albert Narcisse, a Black man, and his brother in a field on Bayou Martin, nine miles from St. Martinsville, Louisiana, and fired on them after they fled to Narcisse's house. Narcisse and a ten-year-old boy were shot, the two men were captured, and the whites reported finding thirty new guns in the cabin. The main dispatch said the captives' fate was unknown, while one condensed version said Narcisse and his son had been fatally shot. Northern papers carried the report under headlines about Louisiana "race troubles" and whites "enraged" at Black residents arming themselves.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Albert Smartt
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Albert Smartt took place on the night of August 16, 1888, when a mob of Black men at Tullahoma, Tennessee, organized to lynch Smartt, a Black prisoner accused of killing his brother-in-law, Samuel Strabler. An officer outwitted the mob and drove Smartt to the jail at Manchester, and the dispatch reporting the episode ran under the headline "A Mob Thwarted."

episodes.title: Lynching of Amos Miller
episodes.lead: The lynching of Amos Miller was the hanging of a Black man accused of assaulting Mrs. Scott, a white woman of Maury County, Tennessee, by an armed mob that seized him in the court room at Franklin, Williamson County, on August 10, 1888. About fifty unmasked men took Miller while his lawyers sought a delay in his trial and hanged him from a railing of the court house in the presence of the court. A coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of unknown parties.

episodes.title: Lynching of Archer Cook
episodes.lead: The lynching of Archer Cook was the killing of a Black man, about 22, whom armed and masked men took from the Prince Edward County jail at Farmville, Virginia, early on August 31, 1888, and hanged and shot. Cook had been jailed for months awaiting trial on a charge of assaulting a young white woman, Lizzie Frank. Wire items carried the news across the Midwest and the Dakotas, and a Leavenworth, Kansas, weekly addressed to Black readers urged them to arm and guard the jails.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Si Bearden
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Si Bearden took place at Springfield, Missouri, in August and September 1888, when mobs surrounded the Springfield jail and threatened to lynch Bearden, a Black man accused of shooting police officer Palmer. Bearden, badly wounded by officers at his capture, was not lynched; after a second mob gathered, Sheriff Dodson moved him to the St. Louis jail for safe keeping. Wire reports of the mob of 300 ran in papers across the country.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Si Beardon
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Si Beardon took place at Springfield, Missouri, in August and September 1888, when mobs surrounded the county jail holding Beardon, a Black man accused of shooting a policeman. No one was lynched, and on September 10 Sheriff Dodson moved Beardon to the St. Louis jail for safekeeping. Wire reports of his capture and his 'narrow escape' ran in papers from Texas to Washington.

episodes.title: Braswell trestle lynching
episodes.lead: The Braswell trestle lynching was the hanging of an unnamed Black man from a railroad trestle at Braswell, Georgia, printed as "Beaswell" in wire reports, on the night of August 25, 1888. He had been accused of "gross immorality" with a Black woman, and an informant told a correspondent that the lynchers were a mixed crowd of white and Black men. Wire dispatches carried the killing to papers as far away as Dakota as a "mysterious lynching."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Ben Bethel
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Ben Bethel took place at Pleasant Hill, in Talbot County, Georgia, on the evening of Sunday, August 5, 1888, when citizens assembled intending to lynch Bethel, a Black man accused of attempted burglary. According to the only report found, "cooler counsel prevailed" and Bethel was sent to jail at Talbotton.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of Ben Brand
episodes.lead: The reported lynching of Ben Brand was the reported hanging, in August 1888, of a Black man near Douglass swamp in Salem, South Carolina, after he had been whipped and ordered to leave the county. The Manning Times and a widely reprinted wire brief said he had been hanged, but the Times later printed its correspondent's report that the hanging never happened and that Brand had only been whipped and banished.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Ben Scott
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Ben Scott took place in Elkhart, Indiana, in August 1888, after Scott was accused of stabbing three men there on August 3. A posse formed to lynch him missed the officers who took him to the jail at Goshen, and after one of the stabbed men, Cornelius Crowley, died on August 6 there was renewed talk of a lynching party. No attack on the jail is reported, and Scott remained in custody.

episodes.title: Lynching near Big Cypress Bayou, Bossier Parish (1888)
episodes.lead: The lynching near Big Cypress Bayou was the hanging of an unnamed Black man by a mob near Big Cypress Bayou in Bossier Parish, Louisiana, on Tuesday, August 14, 1888. He was accused of breaking into a store and stealing a sum of money. The report reached the national press mainly as a short addendum to dispatches about the killing of Black people by 'regulators' near Freetown.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Bill Miles
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Bill Miles was a reported plan in August 1888 by friends of Capt. Nat Kinney, chief of the Bald Knobbers, to lynch Miles, who had shot and killed Kinney in Taney County, Missouri. No attack on Miles was reported; he was released on bond within days and indicted for first-degree murder in October. Papers across the country carried the story because of Kinney's fame as the Bald Knobber founder, warning of "a serious outbreak" if Miles was not hanged.

episodes.title: Lynching of Billy Cole
episodes.lead: The lynching of Billy Cole was the hanging of William "Billy" Cole, accused of shooting two men at a dance, by twelve masked men who took him from the lockup at Guide Rock, Nebraska, early on August 20, 1888. He was hanged from a railroad bridge while both men he had wounded were reported alive, and the lynchers were not identified. Wire reports carried the story nationally the next day, and some Nebraska editors treated it lightly.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bob Broom
episodes.lead: The lynching of Bob Broom was the hanging of a Black man by a crowd of more than 200 men at Utica, Hinds County, Mississippi, on August 13, 1888. Broom had been jailed the night before, accused of leading a party of Black men who shot Dr. L. W. Holliday dead and wounded two other white men after a quarrel over the sidewalk. The story ran across the country, and a month later papers reported that a second accused man, Curtis Shortney, had been taken from a train and was supposed lynched.

episodes.title: Killing of Pap Ryland and threatened lynching of C. A. Babcock
episodes.lead: The killing of Pap Ryland and threatened lynching of C. A. Babcock took place on the Sweetwater in western Colorado in late August 1888, when Babcock shot the aged rancher Ryland and Ryland's neighbors talked of lynching him. Babcock escaped on horseback to Dotsero, took a train to Glenwood Springs and surrendered to a deputy sheriff, and by October he was on trial at Glenwood. Papers treated the case as the death of a pioneer 'character' and as a narrow escape from a mob.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Dan Ritchie
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Dan Ritchie took place in Ashland, Wisconsin, early on August 30, 1888, when a crowd of railroad men gathered intending to take the saloonkeeper from the county jail and lynch him for the shooting of switchman William Amrine. The crowd, reported at nearly 200 men, dispersed after Sheriff Breen warned that armed deputies inside would shoot to kill, and the wire story that carried the news across the country praised him as an example to other sheriffs.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Dave and Albert Lewis
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Dave and Albert Lewis took place in Kentucky in August 1888, when a mob threatened to lynch two young men charged with killing their cousin. The two were taken to the jail at Mt. Sterling because Morgan county had no place secure enough to protect them, and no attack on them was reported. Kentucky papers said the pair had murdered both a young woman and their cousin, while the wire story behind the case gave a different account of who was charged with what.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching near Prosperity, South Carolina
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching near Prosperity, South Carolina, took place in August 1888, when neighbors of Wade H. Suber in Newberry County accused an unnamed Black wagon driver of murdering and robbing him and seriously considered lynching him. The threat ended when Suber was found alive and well at Spartanburg.

episodes.title: Disappearance of Mormon elders Davis and Weaver
episodes.lead: The disappearance of Mormon elders Davis and Weaver occurred in Clay County, Alabama, in August 1888, when two missionaries vanished a day after a body of masked men ordered them to leave the county. A Birmingham dispatch reported that they were "generally believed" to have been murdered by local citizens and their bodies concealed, and a later item credited to the Clay County Leader said flatly that they had been killed. No report of their bodies being found appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Burning of a Mojave woman accused of witchcraft (1888)
episodes.lead: The burning of a Mojave woman accused of witchcraft was the reported killing, in late summer 1888, of an unnamed Mojave woman of about eighteen by members of her tribe in eastern San Bernardino County, California. According to the reports, the band's leaders judged her a witch, and she was tied to a stake and burned, dying after about two hours. The story reached the press through two Los Angeles accounts in mid-September and ran nationally under headlines about Indian "barbarism" and revived witch burning.

episodes.title: Freetown killings (1888)
episodes.lead: The Freetown killings took place on August 16, 1888, when an armed body of white men from three south Louisiana parishes besieged a house in Freetown, a Black settlement in Iberia Parish, and shot dead between ten and twenty Black men who had armed themselves there. One white attacker, the New Iberia civil engineer E. Payson Smith, was killed while forcing the door. The affair became a partisan issue: Southern papers called it a 'war of races', while Northern Republican papers and a senator called it murder.

episodes.title: Fayetteville jail watch of 1888
episodes.lead: The Fayetteville jail watch of 1888 was a confrontation in Fayetteville, North Carolina, in late August 1888, when Black residents gathered at night around the Cumberland County jail holding two Black prisoners accused of assaulting a white woman, and police, white citizens and a militia company dispersed and arrested them. No one was harmed, but the arrested men were bound over to the superior court. White papers treated the affair as an attempted jail delivery and a near 'war of races', while the Charlotte Messenger described it as an effort to protect the prisoners from a rumored lynching.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching at Flovilla, Georgia (1888)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching at Flovilla was an attempt planned in August 1888 by white neighbors in Flovilla, Georgia, to lynch an unnamed Black man accused of assaulting his employer's 10-year-old daughter. Sheriff Beauchamp learned of the plan and carried the prisoner to Atlanta for safe keeping, and the episode survives in a single paragraph of Georgia news.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Frank Dodge
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Frank Dodge took place at Peach Springs, Arizona Territory, on 7 August 1888, when residents prepared to hang Dodge, a railroad section foreman, after he was accused of assaulting the young daughter of a train conductor. The party gave up the plan and let the law take its course, and Dodge was later indicted for rape in Mohave County. Arizona and California papers carried the story, and one Flagstaff paper at first printed the names of the accused and the father reversed.

episodes.title: Killing of Frank Gallup
episodes.lead: The killing of Frank Gallup took place at Shenandoah, Iowa, on the night of August 11, 1888, when militiamen besieging his family's house shot dead a man accused of killing a merchant, F. J. Pine, and a crowd dragged his body through the streets on a rope. The first wire said a mob had hanged him to a tree, and the case circulated as a lynching before fuller dispatches described a militiaman's shot and the dragging of a corpse.

episodes.title: Hanging of a soldier at Gardiner, Montana
episodes.lead: The hanging of a soldier at Gardiner, Montana, took place on August 29, 1888, when townspeople put a rope around the neck of an unnamed army recruit accused of robbing the house of a dead woman and hung him up until he confessed. He survived, the stolen goods were recovered, and he was handed over to his commander for military discipline. Papers across the West and Midwest carried the story as the climax of reports about a troublesome batch of recruits, and a Montana paper said residents regretted he had not been hanged to death.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of George Ostrander
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of George Ostrander occurred at Nebraska City, Nebraska, on the night of August 3, 1888, when a mob called for a rope as officers arrested Ostrander, a painter accused of beating his teenage daughter. Officers hurried him to jail and he was not harmed.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching at Graham, North Carolina (1888)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching at Graham, North Carolina, was a planned attempt in August 1888 to lynch a prisoner held in the Alamance county jail on a charge of criminal assault on a white woman. Sheriff Hamilton learned of the plan and moved the prisoner to the Chatham county jail at Pittsboro, and no violence against him was reported. Days later the prisoner was reported to have broken out of the Pittsboro jail with another man.

episodes.title: Lynching of Graves
episodes.lead: The lynching of Graves was the hanging of a 16-year-old Black boy by a mob near Brownstown, Sevier County, Arkansas, late on the night of Friday, August 24, 1888. He had been accused of assaulting the five-year-old daughter of a white farmer, and the mob took him from the officers who held him. A brief dispatch from Little Rock carried the news to papers across the country, and later summaries gave a different charge.

episodes.title: Lynching of Harrison Spencer
episodes.lead: The lynching of Harrison Spencer was the abduction and killing of a Black farmer and local politician near Longview, Gregg County, Texas, in late August 1888 by a masked band that took him from his home at night. His body was found several days later hanging from a tree on Harris Creek, shot, whipped and mutilated. Papers tied the killing to his break with the Union Labor party, and the case was read into a United States Senate debate as an example of political murder in Texas.

episodes.title: Henderson County abduction of an unknown white man (1888)
