episodes.lead: The Henderson County abduction of an unknown white man was an episode in Henderson County, North Carolina, in early August 1888, in which five Black men reportedly beat a white man senseless and carried him off with a rope. The man was not seen again, five men were jailed at Hendersonville, and the white press reported the case as a lynching "by negroes." A body later seen in the French Broad River near Asheville was supposed to be his, but it was never recovered.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Henry Harrison
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of William Henry Harrison took place in Belleville, New Jersey, on the night of August 4, 1888, when a crowd threatened to lynch Harrison, a Black laborer, after his arrest for the fatal stabbing of William Barnett. Harrison was not harmed; he was committed to the jail in Newark, and a coroner's jury charged him with murder.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Henry Johnson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Henry Johnson took place at Grenada, Mississippi, on the night of August 3, 1888, when a crowd of Water Valley men came to the Grenada jail to hang Johnson, a Black prisoner accused of assaulting a young white woman. Officers had already moved Johnson to a jail in an adjoining county, and the crowd went home without violence. The Grenada papers praised their officers and recorded local doubts that Johnson was guilty.

episodes.title: Lynching of James Stott, James Scott and Jeff Wilson
episodes.lead: The lynching of James Stott, James Scott and Jeff Wilson was the hanging of three men by an armed party in western Apache County, Arizona Territory, on or about August 11, 1888, after a group headed by Deputy Sheriff James D. Houck arrested them. The men were suspected of ambush shootings in the conflict between sheep and cattle raisers in the Tonto Basin, and territorial papers disagreed over whether masked men took them from the posse or the posse hanged them itself.

episodes.title: Killing of Jim Thomas
episodes.lead: The killing of Jim Thomas was the shooting of a Black man by a party of mounted men on a plantation in Georgia on a Wednesday night in August 1888, most likely August 8. The killers and their motive were unknown when the only report appeared, and no arrest or follow-up was found.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Joe Loftin
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Joe Loftin took place at Monticello, Lawrence County, Mississippi, early on Tuesday, August 14, 1888, when about 150 or 200 armed men rode into town to lynch Loftin, an escaped convict held in the county jail. Sheriff D. M. Lee had removed the prisoner the evening before and, by his own account, placed him in the Penitentiary. The sheriff's house was burned that night, and the affair split the county into rival citizens' meetings over whether Lee should resign.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Gist
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John Gist was a series of efforts by armed white crowds in early August 1888 to take Gist, a Black prisoner, from the Union County jail in Union, South Carolina, and kill him. Sheriff Long and his deputies repulsed a mob of about 75 on the night he was jailed, a militia company was ordered to guard the jail, and a larger armed party was talked out of attacking two nights later. Gist was then moved to Columbia, and the case drew a long commentary from Union on lynchers and the law.

episodes.title: Hanging of an army recruit at Gardiner, Montana
episodes.lead: The hanging of an army recruit at Gardiner, Montana, took place on August 29, 1888, when a few men put a noose around the neck of an unnamed soldier accused of stealing from the house of a woman who had just died and hanged him from a beam until he told where he had hidden the goods. He survived and was handed over to his commanding officer, Captain Harris, "more dead than alive." Montana papers presented the episode as the climax of misconduct by a "tough" batch of sixteen recruits, and a condensed version circulated as a filler paragraph in papers from Texas to Virginia into December 1888.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of William and Louis Neglin
episodes.lead: The reported lynching of William and Louis Neglin, spelled "Nagler" in wire reports, was a news story of August 1888 in which a dispatch from Holbrook, Arizona Territory, stated that "outlaws" had lynched the two ranchers in Pleasant Valley, in the Tonto Basin. Within two weeks Arizona papers reported that the story was "not correct": William Neglin appeared alive in Winslow, and Louis, at first missing, was later reported safe. The dispatch ran nationally, but the corrections appeared only in Arizona weeklies, and year-end lists of lynchings still counted the brothers.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of two brakemen at Mapleton, Dakota
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of two brakemen at Mapleton, Dakota, was a confrontation on August 28, 1888, in which a large crowd at the Mapleton depot and the town's city marshal demanded two railroad brakemen accused of causing a tramp's death. The sheriff and district attorney escorting the men refused to give them up, and an inquest jury found that the railroad company was not at fault. The St. Paul Daily Globe reported it under the headline "Ripe for a Lynching."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Nathan M. Reed
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Nathan M. Reed took place at Alexandria City, Alabama, in August 1888, when a lynching party was organized against Reed, a farmer about sixty years old who had been jailed on an accusation of killing his wife. The Alexandria City Rifles were called out to guard the jail, and the reports credited the militia alone with saving his life.

episodes.title: Lynching of Noah Griffin
episodes.lead: The lynching of Noah Griffin was the shooting of a Black man by forty masked men at Ocheeshee, Calhoun County, Florida, on Wednesday, August 15, 1888. Griffin had been accused of writing an insulting note to a young white woman, for which a group of white men had already whipped him and ordered him out of the county. The killing reached papers across the country through a single Apalachicola dispatch, and two papers, in Kansas and Minnesota, printed comments condemning it.

episodes.title: Deer Creek vigilante killing of horse thieves
episodes.lead: The Deer Creek vigilante killing of horse thieves was the reported destruction, around August 31 or September 1, 1888, of a camp of sixteen to eighteen men accused of horse and cattle theft by forty to fifty armed vigilantes in the Public Land Strip, or 'No Man's Land'. Three vigilantes were also reported killed. Carried by wire from Kansas City, the story ran in dozens of papers as a battle in which 'no quarter was asked or given', though no paper in the region could supply particulars.

episodes.title: Lynching of Pony Poe
episodes.lead: The lynching of Pony Poe was the hanging of a Black man by a mob of about 300 men near Bellefontaine, Webster County, Mississippi, in late August 1888. Poe, accused of assaulting three women, was taken from a sheriff's posse on the way to jail and hanged at the scene of the alleged crime. Newspapers across the country carried the story, many noting that he was a former teacher, a leader of the county's Black residents and a recent candidate for public office.

episodes.title: Lynching of two prisoners at Sylvaren, Mississippi
episodes.lead: The lynching of two prisoners at Sylvaren, Mississippi, was the shooting of two Black men in a Smith County jail by a mob in mid-August 1888. The two were among four Black prisoners under arrest, accused of killing a white man named Lee, and were shot dead inside the jail. A brief New Orleans dispatch carried the story to papers from New York and Maine to Dakota, and a Leavenworth, Kansas, paper used it in a campaign appeal against the Democratic party.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Cornie O'Brien and Warren Murphy
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Cornie O'Brien and Warren Murphy took place at Osage, Iowa, in late July and early August 1888, when two youths aged 17 and 15, jailed on a charge of first-degree murder, became the object of 'strong talk of lynching.' They were accused of beating to death Henry Stocum, a 19-year-old orphan, and no attack on them was reported. Midwestern and Plains papers carried the case as an example of youthful violence, and a wire brief about 'threats of lynching the prisoners' ran for more than two weeks.

episodes.title: Lynching of Will Robinson
episodes.lead: The lynching of Will Robinson was the hanging of a Black man by a crowd of about 100 people at Staton's stretch, Tallahatchie County, Mississippi, on the morning of August 8, 1888. Robinson had been accused of attempting to assault a white woman, and the only report found, a Dublin dispatch printed in the Grenada Sentinel, said he confessed before he was hanged "without law or ceremony."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Bohan
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of William Bohan took place at Rockaway Beach, Long Island, New York, on August 3, 1888, when an angry crowd gathered at the police lockup where Bohan, a saloon keeper accused of gouging out his wife's eyes, was held. The crowd dispersed after a constable told it that the prisoner had already been taken away, and Bohan was moved to the Queens County Jail for his safety. The threat was reported only by the New-York Tribune; most papers dwelt instead on the assault, which the Evening World called 'one of the most horrible and fiendish acts ever recorded', and on Bohan's sentence of about twenty-seven years.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Bailey in Crawford County, Arkansas
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Bailey was a night visit in September 1888 by friends of a Black man whom Bailey, an overseer in Crawford County, Arkansas, had shot and killed about a week earlier. The group fled when Bailey came out with a shotgun, and no one was hurt. The only known report, a short state-news item, presented the episode as an anecdote about the rope the would-be lynchers left behind.

episodes.title: Lynching of Curtis Shortney
episodes.lead: The lynching of Curtis Shortney was the seizure of a Black prisoner from a freight train near Utica, Mississippi, on September 12, 1888, by a party that was reported to have lynched him. Shortney was accused of taking part in the killing of Dr. L. W. Holliday at Utica about three weeks earlier, a killing for which Bob Broome had already been hanged by lynchers. The wire dispatch said only that it was "supposed" he was lynched, and no report of his body appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Lynching of Dan Mann
episodes.lead: The lynching of Dan Mann took place at Bartow, Florida, at an unstated date before September 1888. It is known only from a passing remark in a news item about a petition to pardon W. W. Willingham, a convicted murderer whose life Mann, as a juror, was said to have saved.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Mendoza and David Walsh
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Mendoza and David Walsh took place on September 22, 1888, in Sonoma County, California, when residents near Santa Rosa seized two youths accused of burning barns and threatened to lynch them. One dispatch said the pair confessed after being hanged for a short time, but the marshal prevented a lynching, and both were later convicted of arson.

episodes.title: Killing of Ernest Williams
episodes.lead: The killing of Ernest Williams was the fatal shooting of a Black man in Macon, Georgia, on September 4, 1888, as an excited crowd chased him after he ran from an attempted arrest. Accounts of who fired differed, and at the coroner's inquest the next day three Black witnesses named a white man, Daniel Lucas, as the shooter.

episodes.title: Lynching of Frank Gillam and George Elliott
episodes.lead: The lynching of Frank Gillam and George Elliott was the reported hanging of two men accused of horse theft by cowmen in Routt county, Colorado, near the Utah line, in mid-September 1888. The news reached Aspen, where Gillam had lived, as rumor, but papers in Colorado and Montana repeated it as fact.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Frank Polonious
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Frank Polonious occurred about late September 1888 near Mahanoy City, when passengers on a Lehigh Valley passenger train nearly lynched an eighteen-year-old Hungarian caught trying to wreck it with a stone on the track. He was not harmed, and in November he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to three and a half years in prison and a $500 fine.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Fullberg
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Fullberg was an episode in Montana Territory in September 1888, when a man named Fullberg came to the military post at Fort Shaw with his family and asked protection from a body of vigilantes he said meant to lynch him. The commanding officer declined to protect him, calling it a matter for the civil authorities, and no later outcome was reported.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of George Simpson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of George Simpson took place on the night of September 20, 1888, when a crowd of about eighty Black men went to the jail at Fayetteville, West Virginia, and demanded Simpson, a Black prisoner accused of an indecent assault on a white woman. The sheriff had already sent Simpson into the woods with a deputy, and the next morning he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to three years in the penitentiary. Papers in West Virginia and Virginia carried the story under headlines such as "May be a Lynching" and "Ready for the Lynchers."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of George Foster
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of George Foster occurred near Smithfield, Fulton County, Illinois, in September 1888, when Foster, accused of outraging his nine-year-old daughter, was reported to have narrowly escaped lynching before being held in the county jail at Lewistown. He was not harmed, and no crowd or act against him was described. The case drew notice mainly through a Canton dispatch carried in the Northwest and through the Canton Register's open regret that he had not been lynched.

episodes.title: Round Mountain ambush (1888)
episodes.lead: The Round Mountain ambush was a shooting at Round Mountain, Cherokee County, Alabama, in September 1888, in which a white man, George Whitt, and his friends were reported to have fired from ambush on five Black men, killing two and wounding three. An armed battle between the two sides followed later that night, with several people reported killed and wounded on both sides. Newspapers from New York to California ran the report as a "race war."

episodes.title: Killing of Gus Saddler
episodes.lead: The killing of Gus Saddler was the shooting of a young Black man by an unknown person at Bagdad, Calcasieu Parish, Louisiana, on September 2, 1888, while he was held by a crowd of local citizens. The crowd had seized him after he was accused of raping a six-year-old white girl and forced a confession from him by staging a mock hanging. A coroner's jury found that he had been killed by an unknown party, and the Lake Charles Commercial presented the death as "Swift Retribution."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Henry Coleman
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Henry Coleman took place early on September 11, 1888, when a partly masked mob rushed the police station-house in Norfolk, Virginia, to seize Coleman, a Black man held for the murder of a dairyman. Police drove the crowd off, the mayor persuaded it to disperse, and Coleman was moved under military guard to the county jail in Portsmouth. Virginia papers covered the attack at length, including the governor's order that Coleman be protected, while distant papers ran brief notices.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Henry and Jennie Adcock
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Henry and Jennie Adcock took place at Oxford, Granville County, North Carolina, in September 1888, when threats were made to lynch the two white prisoners, who were charged with poisoning Henry Adcock's wife. Judge W. M. Shipp ordered them moved to the jail at Raleigh for safekeeping, and their trial was transferred to Vance County. No attack took place, and the trial was later postponed to February 1889.

episodes.title: Henry County camp-meeting killings
episodes.lead: The Henry County camp-meeting killings were the shooting deaths of seven Black men at a Black camp meeting in Henry County, Alabama, on a night in early September 1888, reportedly Friday, September 7. The killers were described as Milburn, a white man, and his friends, or as masked or unknown white men, and the dead as the supposed ringleaders of an attack on Milburn's house the night before. No arrests had been made when the story ran in papers across the country in the following week.

episodes.title: Lynching threats against John W. Booker
episodes.lead: The lynching threats against John W. Booker were threats made against a sixteen-year-old Black youth after a Democratic political parade in Indianapolis, Indiana, on Saturday night, 22 September 1888. Booker was accused of assaulting a marching member of the Frances Cleveland Club, and an editorial said 'excited Democratic hoodlums' threatened to lynch him. He was not harmed; he was fined in the Mayor's court, and the Republican Indianapolis Journal treated the affair as a partisan overreaction.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jean Pierre Salet and Didaere
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jean Pierre Salet and Didaere was the killing of two Black men by a crowd of armed men at Ville Platte Prairie, near Opelousas in St. Landry Parish, Louisiana, on September 16, 1888. The men were taken from their homes, led a short distance away and shot with buckshot, reportedly because of "incendiary language" they had used. A short Opelousas dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, under headlines that gave the victims' speech as the cause of their deaths.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Jim Dillard
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Jim Dillard took place at a political meeting in Clarendon, Monroe County, Arkansas, on Saturday, September 1, 1888, when a crowd beat and stabbed Dillard, a Black party flag-bearer, after he shot a white man and the sheriff. Two men died in the fight, William Walls and a Black spectator, John Stayton, while Dillard survived and was kept in jail away from Clarendon as armed crowds searched for him. Papers across the country ran the story as an example of violent campaigning in Arkansas.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Baker
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Baker was the reported hanging of a farm hand by his fellow threshing workers on the farm of a man named Weeks near Guide Rock, in Webster County, Nebraska, on September 1, 1888. Baker was accused of feeding the boy who cut bands on the crew into the threshing machine after the boy accidentally cut his hand, and the other hands hanged him from the machine's straw carrier. The story ran nationally under an "Agenda, Kan." dateline, and one Kansas editor called it a fabrication that had fooled the Associated Press.

episodes.title: Mob attack on an Italian prisoner at Corning, New York
episodes.lead: The mob attack on an Italian prisoner at Corning, New York, took place on September 9, 1888, when a crowd of several hundred people stoned and clubbed an Italian laborer whom officers had arrested after the fatal shooting of John King in a saloon. Whether the man survived is disputed: most reports said he was nearly killed, while a later New-York Tribune dispatch said he died in the lockup within minutes. New York papers drew attention to the case because of reports that the crowd had attacked the wrong man.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Nicoli
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John Nicoli was an attack by a mob on the lock-up at Rochester, Pennsylvania, on the night of September 15, 1888, aimed at lynching Nicoli, an Italian charged with assaulting two little girls. Officers removed him through a back window to the jail at Beaver, and no one was reported killed. The episode reached readers across the country only as a brief Pittsburg wire dispatch.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Tanner, John Tanner and Alonzo Smith
episodes.lead: The lynching of Henry Tanner, John Tanner and Alonzo Smith was the hanging of three Black prisoners by a masked crowd that took them from the jail at Oxford, Granville County, North Carolina, at about 2 a.m. on Sunday, September 2, 1888. The Tanners, father and son, were charged with murdering an elderly Black man, Squire Grissom, and Smith with arson or burglary and arson. A Raleigh dispatch called it a lynching "such as was never before recorded in the history of the State."

episodes.title: Eldorado election violence of 1888
episodes.lead: The Eldorado election violence of 1888 was a series of attacks on Black voters by armed white men at Eldorado, the seat of Union County, Arkansas, on election day, Monday, September 3, 1888, and the nights before it. According to Union County white men quoted from Little Rock, about 100 armed men guarded the roads into town, killed one Black man, and beat and bayoneted another, Jordan Gray, who was left confined to his bed. Republican and Union Labor sources blamed Democrats and gave death counts ranging from one to sixteen.

episodes.title: Lynching of Lewis Davis
episodes.lead: The lynching of Lewis Davis was the hanging of a jailed prisoner by a masked mob in Crawford County, Missouri, early on Sunday, September 23, 1888. Davis, awaiting trial for the murder of his neighbor David Miller, was taken from jail and hanged over the grave of Pat Wallace, whom a mob had lynched two years before. The papers dwelt on his fight in his cell, and the judge ordered a special grand jury.

episodes.title: Lynching of Lewis Davis
episodes.lead: The lynching of Lewis Davis took place early on September 23, 1888, when a masked mob broke into the jail at Steelville, Missouri, and hanged Davis, who was awaiting trial for the murder of farmer David Miller. He was hanged over the grave of Pat Wallace, lynched in the same county in 1886, a detail that headlined the coverage. Judge Bland ordered a special grand jury, but no report of its findings appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Killing of Martin Wilson
episodes.lead: The killing of Martin Wilson was the shooting of a Black man by a posse at a place printed as Malton, Alabama, reported at the end of August 1888. He was accused of having attempted to assault a white woman, and the only known report gave that accusation as the reason he was killed.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Michael Reinhart
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Michael Reinhart took place at Winamac, Indiana, on the evening of September 13, 1888, after Reinhart, a barber, shot and killed the contractor Joseph W. Robinson in a saloon. A crowd threatened to lynch him, and the sheriff guarded the jail with a large force until the danger passed. Reinhart was convicted of murder two months later and sentenced to life imprisonment.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Monroe Wilkinson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Monroe Wilkinson took place at Scottsville, Allen County, Kentucky, on the night of Sunday, September 23, 1888, when a party of about forty Black men twice tried to take Wilkinson from the town jail and hang him. Wilkinson, a Black man, was accused of shooting an elderly Black man in the back during a church service. The attackers were driven off, and the story ran nationally as a wire item about a murder in a church and a lynching threatened by Black residents.

episodes.title: Lynching of Wise in the Turtle Mountains
episodes.lead: The lynching of Wise was the hanging of a man reported only as Wise by settlers in the Turtle Mountains of Dakota Territory in mid-September 1888, after they accused him of stealing their horses. The news reached the national press through a single Bismarck dispatch, which papers headlined less for the lynching itself than for the claim that the dead man had once been a prominent citizen of Wyoming.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Perry Drake
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Perry Drake took place in September 1888 at Spencer, Roane County, West Virginia, where a mob tried to take Drake, on trial for the murder of the Rev. Thomas Ryan, from officers and threatened to lynch him. Threats against him continued in court and on the streets until the jury failed to agree, and no one was killed. Wire dispatches carried the story to papers as far away as New York and Ohio under headlines promising a lynching.

episodes.title: Alleged lynching of Press Sams
episodes.lead: The alleged lynching of Press Sams was an unconfirmed report, printed in white newspapers in October 1888, that Sams, a Black man who had married a white woman near Jacksonville, Illinois, had been lynched in Kentucky. The claim rested on hints from the deputy, D. C. McCoy, as relayed by a Philadelphia Press special, while other reports of the same days said Sams had fled to escape lynching or had left for parts unknown. The coverage dwelt mainly on the marriage across the color line.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Press Sams
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Press Sams was the reported flight of Press Sams, a Black hired man described in the papers as a "mulatto" and a "negro," from would-be lynchers near Moscow, Kentucky, in late September 1888, after he eloped with and married Hattie Flack, the white daughter of a St. Louis commission merchant. A deputy sheriff from Jacksonville, Illinois, tracked the couple to Kentucky and brought Flack back to her family, while wire reports said Sams "fled to escape lynching." One dispatch said the deputy hinted that Sams had been lynched, but other accounts said he escaped or left the country.

episodes.title: 1888 election violence in Union County, Arkansas
episodes.lead: The 1888 election violence in Union County, Arkansas, was a series of floggings, beatings and reported killings of Black men by armed Democrats around the state election of September 3, 1888, centered on El Dorado. Press Neal, Sandy Newton and Aaron Cobb were among the men named as whipped, while the dead went unnamed and estimates ran from one or two Black men to a rumored sixteen. Northern Republican papers held up the county as an example of how the Democrats had carried Arkansas.

episodes.title: Killing of Robert Chun
episodes.lead: The killing of Robert Chun was the reported fatal shooting of a Black man by a policeman in Birmingham, Alabama, on the morning of September 2, 1888. Accused of taking goods from a dry goods store, Chun fled from several policemen and was shot at by Policeman Oldham, and a Memphis paper reported the episode under the headline "Killed a Fleeing Burglar."

episodes.title: Lynching of Sam Cornwall
episodes.lead: The lynching of Sam Cornwall was the shooting death of a Black prisoner on a public road in Chester County, South Carolina, in the early morning of September 29 or 30, 1888, while he was in a constable's custody on a peace warrant. His guard said they were fired on from ambush and fled, and a coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of parties unknown. Papers from New York to Texas carried the story, several of them blaming the officers who had left him.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Sam Long
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Sam Long refers to a September 1888 report that Long, a Black man from Georgia held by officers at Eufaula, Alabama, would likely be lynched if returned to Miller County, Georgia, where he was wanted on a charge of assaulting a white woman. The only report found, a brief in the Savannah Morning News, said his chances for a trial were "thought to be slim"; no account of his fate appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Breaux Bridge night raid
episodes.lead: The Breaux Bridge night raid was an attack on the night of September 14, 1888, in which four or five armed men went to Black cabins near Breaux Bridge, Louisiana, killed a Black woman, whipped a Black man, and sexually assaulted a Black woman. Five men were arrested; one, Sam Polk, turned state's witness and named Vilmont Hollier as the man who fired, and two were held without bail. The killing was carried by wire across the country and was cited in the United States Senate as political violence.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of Press Sams
episodes.lead: The reported lynching of Press Sams was a rumor, carried in wire reports of October 1-2, 1888, that a Black coachman who had married Hattie Flack, a white merchant's daughter from near Jacksonville, Illinois, had been lynched by whites near Clinton, Kentucky. The story rested on Deputy Sheriff D. C. McCoy, who brought Flack home to St. Louis and would not say what had become of Sams but intimated that he had been lynched. Other reports, including a dispatch from Clinton, said Sams had fled or had deserted his wife before her arrest, and no confirmation of a killing appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Lynching of Sherman Farrior
episodes.lead: The lynching of Sherman Farrior took place in Whiteville, Columbus County, North Carolina, on the night of September 12, 1888, when a body of a hundred or more men took Farrior, a Black prisoner, from the county jail and hanged him from an oak tree. Farrior was awaiting trial on a charge of outraging an aged white woman. North Carolina papers counted the hanging as the thirteenth lynching in the state that year, and reports differed on whether the mob was made up of masked men of unstated race or of Black men.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Sylvester Grubb
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Sylvester Grubb consisted of mob efforts in Gibson County, Indiana, in September and October 1888 to seize and hang Grubb, who was accused of shooting Gertrude Downey at the Princeton fair grounds. Officials kept Grubb out of reach by moving him to Evansville and Jeffersonville, and a mob of sixty masked men that searched a train for him at Francisco found the wrong train. Grubb was instead tried in the Knox Circuit Court at Vincennes and sentenced to death.

episodes.title: Killing of T. C. Yates
episodes.lead: The killing of T. C. Yates was the shooting of a man described as "a noted desperado" in the Chickasaw Nation, Indian Territory, on or about September 1, 1888. According to a wire dispatch from Little Rock, Arkansas, Yates fired into a crowd, people in the crowd fired back, and he fell dead from his horse. Papers across the country printed the item as a short brief, and one Kentucky paper condensed it to a line saying he had been "killed by a mob."

episodes.title: Lynching of Thomas Reese
episodes.lead: The lynching of Thomas Reese was the killing of a Black man, also called Samuel Long, by a crowd at Moultrie, Colquitt County, Georgia, on September 4, 1888. Accused of assault and attempted poisoning, he was taken after a court ordered him committed, then mutilated, hanged and shot in daylight by unmasked men.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Victor Sebree
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Victor Sebree took place at Rio Grande City, Starr County, Texas, in September 1888, when armed Mexican residents tried to seize Sebree, a United States customs officer, after he shot the editor Catarino E. Garza in a street fight. Sebree escaped to Fort Ringgold, whose commander refused to give him up, while the crowd held the town and cut its telegraph line. No one was killed, and papers across the country reported the episode as a border uprising threatening a "massacre" of American citizens.

episodes.title: Lynching of William Martin
episodes.lead: The lynching of William Martin was the killing of a Black man near Rome, Covington County, Alabama, in late summer 1888, after he was taken from a deputy sheriff who was moving him to Florida. Martin, accused of assaulting a white woman, was shot and his body thrown into an old well, and the story ran as a brief wire item in Georgia and Kansas papers.

episodes.title: Lynching of William Lewis
episodes.lead: The lynching of William Lewis was the hanging of a Black man by unknown persons near Durant, Mississippi, whose body was found on a tree on the morning of September 4, 1888. No cause was assigned and the perpetrators were not identified. The case reached readers only as a brief wire item, printed in Savannah and in several Northern papers the next day.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Merriwether
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of William Merriwether took place in Atlanta, Georgia, on the night of September 29, 1888, when a crowd of Black men called for hanging him after he fatally cut Marion Cunningham in an Ivy street billiard saloon. Police kept Merriwether from the crowd, and in November a jury convicted him of murder and fixed his penalty at life on the chain-gang. The New York Sun described the crowd as a mob "determined on lynching him," though other reports treated the case as a killing over cards.

episodes.title: Lynching of Wise (Dakota, 1888)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Wise was the hanging of an accused horse thief by settlers in the Turtle Mountains of Dakota on Wednesday, September 12, 1888. According to accounts relayed from Bismarck, several settlers who had missed horses overtook him on his way to Manitoba, disarmed him, and hanged him from the nearest tree. Papers across the country carried the story because the dead man was said to have once been a prominent citizen of Wyoming mentioned for its legislature.

episodes.title: Lynching of Aaron Bean
episodes.lead: The lynching of Aaron Bean took place near Jasper, Texas, on Wednesday, October 3, 1888, when a mob took Bean, a Black man, from officers on the road to jail and shot him to death. Bean had been accused of accosting the young daughter of a Magnolia Springs farmer while she was riding and dragging her from her saddle. The killing was known outside Texas through a single Galveston wire dispatch, which several papers printed under headlines approving of it.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Amsley O'Dell
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Amsley O'Dell took place on the night of October 27, 1888, at the railroad depot in Greenville, Ohio, when a crowd of Dayton men tried to lynch O'Dell after he shot a bystander during a fight that followed a Democratic political meeting. Officers and citizens hid him in the depot cellar while the mob wrecked the building, and he was then jailed. The bystander, James M. Powell, died of his wound on November 9, and O'Dell was held on bond for the grand jury.

episodes.title: Killings of Jim Bell, Ben Russell and George W. Griffin
episodes.lead: The killings of Jim Bell, Ben Russell and George W. Griffin took place on Wednesday night, October 31, 1888, in Van Zandt County, Texas, when four white men who had gone to arrest Russell on a misdemeanor charge shot him and two companions before, according to the reports, they could obey an order to raise their hands. Accounts disagreed on whether one, two or three of the Black men died, and friends of the dead claimed that the shooting was political. Three of the four white men were arrested, charged with murder and released on bond, and a wire dispatch carried the story across the country.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of the Wilkin brothers
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of the Wilkin brothers took place at Breeze, Illinois, in late October 1888, when Henry, Ben and John Wilkin, arrested for stabbing a man in a saloon row, were reported to have narrowly escaped being lynched. No one was killed, and the episode survives only in a one-sentence item in the Indianapolis Journal.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bill Johnson
episodes.lead: The lynching of Bill Johnson took place near Cochran, Georgia, on Saturday, October 13, 1888, when a crowd of men hanged Johnson, a Black farm hand, from a tree a mile from town and riddled his body with bullets. Johnson had been accused of outraging the wife of the farmer who employed him, and the crowd left a placard on his body reading "Our women must and shall be protected." A wire dispatch carried the story to papers across the country within two days.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Bill Short
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Bill Short followed the fatal shooting of Mrs. Alma Barnes, a 19-year-old widow, at a dance in Litchfield, Kansas, on the night of October 27, 1888. Short, a miner, was accused of shooting her after she refused to let him escort her home, and he was removed to Girard because of threats of lynching. No report of an attack on Short appears in the coverage, which consisted of one wire dispatch reprinted across the country.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Thomas Brown
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Thomas Brown took place shortly after midnight on October 19, 1888, when a mob of several hundred men went to the county jail at Moorhead, Minnesota, to hang Brown, a prisoner accused of shooting a Moorhead policeman. Sheriff Jensen had removed Brown earlier in the evening, and the mob dispersed after a committee searched the jail and failed to find him. The episode was reported in papers from Minnesota to Montana and Michigan, mostly in a wire version that placed the mob at Fargo, and a second threatened lynching at Moorhead followed in November.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Thomas Brown at Moorhead, Minnesota
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Thomas Brown took place shortly after midnight on October 18-19, 1888, when a mob of several hundred men went to the county jail at Moorhead, Minnesota, to lynch a prisoner accused of killing a policeman. Sheriff Jensen had already removed the wounded prisoner, and the crowd dispersed after a committee searched the jail. Papers across the Midwest and Northwest carried the story, and one wire report commended the sheriff.

episodes.title: Killing of Caesar Stevens
episodes.lead: The killing of Caesar Stevens was the shooting of a Black laborer by a group of armed white men in a garden at Branchville, South Carolina, on October 8, 1888. Stevens was struck nine times and died the next morning, and the three men named as the shooters were not arrested in the days that followed. Papers in South Carolina and Georgia called it a cold-blooded murder and singled out the lack of arrests.

episodes.title: Shooting of Police Chief Hayes and threatened lynching at Crookston, Minnesota
episodes.lead: The shooting of Police Chief Hayes and threatened lynching at Crookston, Minnesota, followed an attack on the night of October 19, 1888, in which a man described as a tramp fired six shots at Hayes from behind. The shooter was arrested at once, and newspapers reported 'strong talk of lynching' him, but no attack on the jail was reported, and in December he was convicted in court.

episodes.title: Shooting of Alfred Williams
episodes.lead: The shooting of Alfred Williams was an attack on a Black pastor near Edgewood, Georgia, who was found in the woods on the morning of October 11, 1888, with over a hundred buckshot wounds that an Atlanta dispatch attributed to members of his own congregation. The dispatch said he was expected to die, and several papers headlined the story as a lynching or murder, but no report of his death was found.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Joseph Barrett
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Joseph Barrett took place in Elkhart, Indiana, on October 27, 1888, when a crowd tried to seize a police officer who had just shot and killed a fellow officer, William Burton. The sheriff held Barrett in a saloon while the mayor and sheriff spoke to the crowd, a rainstorm scattered it, and Barrett was driven to the county jail at Goshen. The killing of one officer by another and the near-lynching that followed ran as a wire story in papers from Minnesota to California and the Dakotas.

episodes.title: Lynching of Thomas Sayers
episodes.lead: The lynching of Thomas Sayers took place near Bramwell, Mercer County, West Virginia, around the beginning of November 1888, when a mob took Sayers, a Black man accused of leading a highway robbery, from officers taking him to jail and hanged him from a tree. He had been held for the grand jury after an attack on four white produce sellers in which two were shot. A Post-Dispatch wire carried the news nationally under headlines such as "Negro Murderer Lynched," though reports differed on the date, on whether the robbery victims died, and on how many men were lynched.

episodes.title: Lynching of F. W. Adams and Charles Lutzier
episodes.lead: The lynching of F. W. Adams and "Dutchy" was the hanging of two hunters by masked settlers on the Snake River in Carbon County, Wyoming Territory, in October 1888. Accused of slaughtering elk and deer for their hides and of burning a ranchman's house, the two were taken from a guarded adobe hut and hanged from a tree. Later reports of mutilation, fleeing witnesses and freed suspects led Wyoming papers to call it "one of the most atrocious outrages ever committed in Wyoming territory."

episodes.title: Lynching of Frank Easterling
episodes.lead: The lynching of Frank Easterling took place on the night of Saturday, October 6, 1888, in Rankin County, Mississippi, when a mob took Easterling, a Black man, out and hanged him and shot Sharper Easterling, at whose house he was found. Mississippi papers gave two motives: the first reports said Frank was killed for saying he would vote Democratic, while later briefs said he was accused of stealing cotton.

episodes.title: Appomattox mob of 1888
episodes.lead: The Appomattox mob of 1888 was the seizure and threatened lynching of Gen. T. T. (Thomas) Taylor and Col. J. A. Grayson, of Hutchinson, by armed residents of Appomattox, Grant County, Kansas, after the town lost a county-seat election to Ulysses in October 1888. Accused of selling the town out, the two men were held under guard, threatened with hanging and made to sign over deeds and checks before they got away unharmed. Papers across the country carried it as a county-seat election that nearly ended in a lynching.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of George Williams and Charles Crandall
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of George Williams and Charles Crandall followed the arrest of the two men, one described as "colored" and the other as white, on charges of breaking into the home of an elderly couple outside Middletown, Connecticut, near Durham, on October 23, 1888, and assaulting the wife. A New Haven wire dispatch reported "threats of lynching them," but no crowd or move against the prisoners appears in the coverage. Both men were indicted for rape and in December were sentenced to fifteen years in state prison.

episodes.title: Greensburg jail fire
episodes.lead: The Greensburg jail fire destroyed the wooden jail at Greensburg, Louisiana, on the night of October 31 or November 1, 1888, killing its only prisoner, a Black youth held on a charge of horse stealing. The cause of the fire was not reported, and the story circulated nationally as a one-sentence wire brief.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Henry Granel
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Henry Granel occurred on the evening of October 25, 1888, at Sheepshead Bay, Long Island, New York, when villagers threatened to lynch a hotel keeper arrested for striking a teenage jockey with a baseball bat. Police held the crowd back with drawn revolvers and took Granel to a cell at Coney Island, and no one was killed. Daily papers treated the assault as a notably brutal crime, while weekly digests reported that Granel had been "narrowly saved from lynching."

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Jones
episodes.lead: The lynching of Henry Jones took place near Woodland Mills, in Obion County, Tennessee, on the night of October 26, 1888, when a mob killed Jones, a Black man. A Nashville wire dispatch said he had murdered a white man, while a Kentucky weekly, the Hickman Courier, said he had shot at a man and wounded his horse, and that he was taken from officers and hanged. The two-sentence wire item ran in papers from Virginia to Washington Territory, and no report of an inquest or arrests appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Lynching of Hickman
episodes.lead: The lynching of Hickman was the killing of a man named Hickman by a mob of about seventy-five men at Boston, Colorado, in early October 1888. Hickman was accused of having shot and killed J. C. Booth, a man who had been visiting the woman Hickman lived with, and the mob took him from his house within hours and hanged him. The story reached the national press as a brief Trinidad dispatch and was reprinted in papers from Georgia to Dakota over the following two weeks.

episodes.title: Mob hunt for Huffman, Tiffin, Ohio
episodes.lead: The mob hunt for Huffman was a threatened lynching near Tiffin, Ohio, in October 1888, when a mob of men searched for a man named Huffman, accused of assaulting a six-year-old girl, with the stated intent of lynching him. The only reports are one wire dispatch, and none says whether he was caught.

episodes.title: Fulton church shooting
episodes.lead: The Fulton church shooting was the killing of Nina (or Mina) Emmerson, a Black woman, by her husband, Jackson Emmerson, during a service at the Pilgrims' Rest Church in Fulton, Missouri, on the night of October 22, 1888. Emmerson was jailed amid reported "strong threats of lynching him," but no attack on the jail was reported, and early in November he broke out of the Fulton jail with another prisoner held for murder. A brief wire dispatch carried the shooting to papers across the country, and at least one headlined it as a case for lynching.

episodes.title: Killing of James W. Edloe
episodes.lead: The killing of James W. Edloe was the fatal shooting of a Black political officeholder by Williamsburg, Virginia, policeman A. T. Clowes on the night of October 13, 1888. Clowes claimed self-defense, a coroner's jury found that he fired the fatal shot, and he was jailed, examined, and later released on $3,000 bail. Papers noted the large Black crowds that gathered, and one dispatch said a lynching of the officer was feared.

episodes.title: Lynching of Joe Joiner
episodes.lead: The lynching of Joe Joiner took place at Hutto, Texas, near Taylor and Round Rock, in mid-October 1888, when a mob of masked men hanged Joiner, a Black man, to a tree. Joiner had been accused of attempting to assault a young white girl and had been captured and placed in the hands of the sheriff or officers. A Taylor dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, one of which headlined it "A Negro Brute Hanged by a Mob."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of John Carter
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of John Carter took place in October 1888 at Mayfield, Kentucky, where a crowd cried "lynch him" during the examining trial of Carter, a butcher's son accused of murdering the horse trader William Trafford. Officers removed Carter to the jail at Paducah, which was heavily guarded against an expected mob, and no attack on him was reported.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Kirkland
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Kirkland was the killing of a prisoner by masked men near the jail at Nashville, Arkansas, on the night of October 8, 1888. Kirkland, accused of firing on a local physician, was taken from a constable and shot to death. Brief wire dispatches carried the story to papers in Dakota Territory and Kansas.

episodes.title: Pittsville church shooting
episodes.lead: The Pittsville church shooting was an attack in October 1888 in which a crowd of armed young white men rode up to a Black church at Pittsville, in Fort Bend County, Texas, called the congregation out and fired into it. Lamar Johnson was killed and Taylor Randon was wounded. The Galveston News called it a political assassination and blamed the Jay Bird Club, a new Democratic organization, while a leading Fort Bend Democrat denied that politics played any part.

episodes.title: Lynching of Lewis Edwards
episodes.lead: The lynching of Lewis Edwards was the killing of a Black prisoner by masked men in the county jail at Jesup, Wayne County, Georgia, at about 3 a.m. on October 15, 1888. Edwards had been brought back from confinement to stand a new trial for the 1886 killing of a Jesup hotel proprietor when the men overpowered his guards and shot him in his cell. A coroner's jury attributed his death to an unknown unlawful mob, and the Atlanta Constitution's correspondent called it the first lynching on record in the county.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Smith in Todd County, Kentucky
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Smith in Todd County, Kentucky, followed the killing of a woman and her child near Guthrie on Saturday, October 27, 1888, for which her husband, described as "a colored man named Smith," was blamed in wire reports. Smith was caught after trying to drown himself and was jailed at Springfield, Tennessee, where, a dispatch said, feeling against him was so strong "that he may be lynched." No attack on him appears in the coverage, but the story ran widely as a one-paragraph wire item under headlines such as "A Negro Fiend."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Martin near Fort Hanson
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Martin near Fort Hanson was a pursuit in New Mexico Territory in 1888 in which a posse chased a dentist named Martin, accused of chloroforming and raping a servant girl, intending to lynch him. Martin escaped into the Sacramento mountains, was later arrested in Arizona, and was convicted and sentenced to five years in the penitentiary.

episodes.title: Lynching of Nat Nathaniel
episodes.lead: The lynching of Nat Nathaniel was the hanging of a Black man by a crowd near Brazoria, Texas, in October 1888, after he was accused of shooting Isaac Van Dorn, a plantation engineer. Citizens captured Nathaniel at Wharton, but on the road to the Brazoria jail, about five miles from Brazoria, a crowd took him from his captors and hanged him. The wire story dwelt less on the hanging than on reported threats of retaliation by Black residents, and headlines spoke of a feared race war.

episodes.title: Lynching at Marion, Louisiana (1888)
episodes.lead: The lynching at Marion, Louisiana, was the hanging of an unnamed Black man by a party of men pursuing a suspect in the killing of Luther Hayes, a white man, around October 29, 1888. The man was said to have been implicated in the killing in some way, while the accused shooter, Nathan Broadnax, remained at large. The only known report, carried by the Ouachita Telegraph of Monroe, also passed on expectations that more Black men near Marion would be killed.

episodes.title: Lynching threat against Olson at Bangor, Dakota Territory
episodes.lead: The lynching threat against Olson at Bangor was a declaration by farmers near Bangor, Walworth County, Dakota Territory, in October 1888 that they would hang a farmer named Olson, who was accused of beating and kicking his wife until she lay in critical condition. Dispatches from Aberdeen on October 9 and 10 carried the threat to papers in Dakota, Illinois, Nebraska and Washington, D.C., some under headlines that approved of it. No English-language paper reported the outcome, but a Swedish-language weekly in St. Paul reported in late November that Olson had been lynched.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of R. H. Kruger
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of R. H. Kruger was a reported threat of mob violence against a man arrested in Chicago on October 18, 1888, on a charge of assaulting a girl in Grand Rapids, Michigan. A Chicago wire dispatch quoted a Grand Rapids deputy sheriff as saying Kruger would be lynched if brought back, but no crowd or attack was reported, and a Michigan paper recorded his court appearance the next day without mentioning any threat. Accounts differed over the age and identity of the complainant, and Kruger was later released.

episodes.title: Lynching of Sam Smith
episodes.lead: The lynching of Sam Smith took place near Forney, Texas, on October 25, 1888, when armed and masked men took Smith, a Black man accused of rape, from officers taking him to jail at Kaufman and hanged and shot him. A coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of unknown persons, and Black residents refused to let him be buried in their graveyard. Texas papers noted the speed of the killing, which came less than a day after the alleged crime.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of a train crew at Smith's Mines
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of a train crew at Smith's Mines took place on October 10, 1888, when a crowd of Black miners at Smith's mines, eight miles from Birmingham, Alabama, surrounded the crew of a Birmingham Mineral Railroad freight train, swore to lynch them and fired on their engine as they fled. The crowd had gathered after the train ran over and killed a Black woman, Clara Dickson, and the crew shoveled her remains off the track. None of the crew was hit, and the story ran in papers from New York to Kansas as a narrow escape from a "negro mob."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Sylvester Grubb
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Sylvester Grubb took place on the night of Thursday, October 11, 1888, when armed and masked men boarded and searched a passenger train at Francisco, Gibson County, Indiana, looking for Grubb, who was charged with the murder of Gertrude Downey. Grubb was not aboard, having been taken to Vincennes by another route, and the men left the train without harming anyone. A Princeton wire report carried the story to papers in Pennsylvania, Texas and Delaware as a lynching "narrowly averted".

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Walter Howard
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Walter Howard took place in Jackson, Tennessee, in late October and early November 1888, after Howard, a Black porter for the Southern Express Company, was accused of robbing the company's office and shooting a policeman. After his arrest at Paris, Tennessee, on November 1, a Memphis paper reported "some talk of lynching" in Jackson, but no mob action against him appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of John Andrew Johnson
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of John Andrew Johnson took place in Crockett, Houston County, Texas, in 1888, when crowds sought to take the Black youth from jail while he awaited trial on a charge of raping a white girl. An Austin dispatch of October 11 described a large mob besieging the jail and the governor sending the adjutant general, but a Crockett correspondent called that account mistaken. Johnson was not lynched; he was tried, sentenced to death, and hanged by the state on December 21.

episodes.title: Killing of Silas Jeffries and Abe Davis
episodes.lead: The killing of Silas Jeffries and Abe Davis was a reprisal killing near Tushomma, Indian Territory, in November 1888, in which armed friends of a murdered stockman, William Durant, hunted down and killed two neighbors suspected of leading the party that shot him. Known only from a single Little Rock wire dispatch, the story ran in papers from Washington to Minnesota, and the Washington Evening Star headlined it as a lynching.

episodes.title: Lynching of Archibald Pelon
episodes.lead: The lynching of Archibald Pelon took place at Grayling, Michigan, in the early hours of November 7, 1888, when masked men took him from the sheriff and hanged him from a beam between two trees. Pelon had been arrested for allegedly assaulting two women near Beaver Creek, and no arrests for his killing were reported. The fullest wire dispatch noted that Michigan had seen no lynching in fifteen years.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of August Richards
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of August Richards took place on 11 November 1888 at Halleck, Elko County, Nevada, when five men with a gallows prepared entered a train car and demanded Richards, who was accused of beating and robbing an elderly local man, from the constable taking him to jail. The constable refused, and the men left without the prisoner. The Elko Independent reported the scene with amusement, and a Winnemucca paper said Richards had narrowly escaped lynching.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Charles Burkhart
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Charles Burkhart took place in Wenona, Illinois, on November 12, 1888, when townsmen sought to seize and lynch him as the suspected murderer of the banker Peter Howe and his wife. Burkhart cut his throat with a razor as the crowd closed on his rooms, and two later reports described him as a man of mixed race. Papers across the country carried the story under headlines such as "Judge Lynch Cheated" and "Saved the Lynchers Trouble."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Sid Black
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Sid Black was an attack near Charlotte, North Carolina, on the night of November 2, 1888, in which a crowd of Black men seized a Black man who had declared himself a Democrat, bound him, and put a rope around his neck. Other men intervened before he could be hanged, and some of the crowd were reported arrested. Papers in Richmond, New York and Durham carried the story as part of Charlotte dispatches on the political excitement before the November 6 election.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bob Bonner
episodes.lead: The lynching of Bob Bonner took place at Petersburg, Tennessee, on the night of Friday, November 16, 1888, when five armed masked men took Bonner, a Black prisoner, from the town jail and hanged him half a mile from town. He had been arrested the night before on a charge of outraging a twelve-year-old Black girl. A Nashville wire brief carried the news to papers from Virginia to Minnesota and New Hampshire, while a Tennessee weekly called it "a first class lynching."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Brown, alias Murphy
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Brown, alias Murphy, was a rumored mob attack on a prisoner accused of killing a police officer in Moorhead, Minnesota, which the sheriff forestalled by moving him out of the jail on the night of November 20, 1888. Friends of the dead officer, Pete Poull, were said to be planning to lead a mob at 3 a.m. to lynch him, but no gathering at the jail was reported. It was the second mob threat against the same prisoner in five weeks, following an October crowd that searched the Moorhead jail for him.

episodes.title: Shooting of David Kenney and manhunt for Charles Johnson
episodes.lead: The shooting of David Kenney and manhunt for Charles Johnson took place at Gadsden, Alabama, on about November 12, 1888, when Officer Kenney was fatally shot while trying to make an arrest and some 150 men set out after the accused man. A wire dispatch predicted that Johnson would be lynched if caught, but no report of his capture or fate was found.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Clifton Holden
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Clifton Holden took place at Redwood Falls, Minnesota, on November 26, 1888, when townspeople angered by the murder of his cousin, the Morton barber Frank Dodge, were expected to take him from the village lockup. Warned of trouble, Sheriff Mead of Redwood County moved Holden by train to the jail at New Ulm, and no harm to him was reported. Papers in St. Paul, New Ulm and as far away as Sacramento carried the story, which differed on whether a mob actually reached the prisoner.

episodes.title: Lynching of Davis Sabini
episodes.lead: The lynching of Davis Sabini was the hanging of a 22-year-old Italian man by residents of Cortez, Nevada, in November 1888, after he was accused of fatally shooting Richard "Dick" Holt in a quarrel over a loan. The men involved told a deputy sheriff that Sabini had hanged himself, and a coroner's jury returned a verdict of suicide that the Elko Independent openly doubted. The story ran as a brief wire item in papers across the country, and in Cortez it led the town's Italian residents to threaten revenge.

episodes.title: 1888 Donaldsonville lynching
episodes.lead: The 1888 Donaldsonville lynching was the hanging of an unnamed Black man by a crowd that took him from a jailer near Donaldsonville, Louisiana, in mid-November 1888, after he was accused of assaulting an eleven-year-old white girl on a nearby plantation. The account, a special dispatch to the New Orleans Times-Democrat, was reprinted across the country over the next nine days under headlines such as "A Wretch Lynched" and "Black Flend Lynched."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching near Franklin, Tennessee (1888)
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching near Franklin, Tennessee, in 1888 was a reported threat against an unnamed Black man said to have tried to stop the buggy horse of two young women outside the town. The women escaped, and a brief published on 22 November 1888 said the man would be lynched if caught, but no capture or lynching was reported.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of George Witherell
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of George Witherell occurred at Canon City (also printed Canyon City), Colorado, on the night of November 2, 1888, when a crowd that a Pueblo dispatch put at five hundred people met incoming trains at the station intending to lynch Witherell, who was accused of murdering Charles McCain. The crowd searched one train and broke open the baggage car of another, but Witherell was not aboard. The episode appeared as a short item in a few papers, attached to wider coverage of the killing of which Witherell was accused.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Cook
episodes.lead: The lynching of Henry Cook took place on the night of Sunday, November 11, 1888, in the swamps of Miller County, Georgia, where a group of men ran him down and killed him. Cook had been accused of breaking into a widow's home while drunk and assaulting her 12-year-old daughter. The killing was known only through a short dispatch from Bainbridge, Georgia, which ran in a few papers in Tennessee, Kentucky and Florida.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Jack Barnett
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Jack Barnett took place near Catawba Junction, South Carolina, in late November 1888, when parties of men sought to lynch Barnett, a young Black man accused of assaulting a girl. His captors brought him alive to the Yorkville jail, though a later Columbia dispatch said he might be lynched at any moment.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Jack Hemphill
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Jack Hemphill took place at Gainesville, Georgia, on a Friday night in November 1888, when a crowd gathered to lynch Hemphill, a Black man held in the town lock-up. The marshal reached the lock-up ahead of the crowd and spirited the prisoner away, and no one was reported hurt.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jack Jones
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jack Jones was the hanging of a Black man by a mob at or near Rockwood, Tennessee, reported as having taken place on Thursday, November 22, 1888. Jones was accused of assaulting, or attempting to assault, two women who lived near Rockwood. The story travelled only as one-sentence telegraph and column items, which ran in papers from New York and New Jersey to Mississippi and Louisiana over the following week.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of James Curby
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of James Curby happened at Versailles, Kentucky, on Wednesday, November 7, 1888, when a mob of Black residents chased and captured Curby, a Black man accused of raping a six-year-old girl. Town authorities took him from the mob and jailed him, and the dispatch reported threats to storm the jail.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of James Mills
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of James Mills took place at West Chester, Pennsylvania, on November 20, 1888, when a hostile crowd met Mills, a Black man, as officers brought him to the Chester county prison. Mills was accused of assaulting and trying to drown Bertie Howard, an 11-year-old girl, near Paoli in September. He reached the jail unharmed and was given a hearing the same evening, and the papers dwelt mainly on his confession.

episodes.title: Killing of Jeff Davis's wife at Lake City
episodes.lead: The killing of Jeff Davis's wife at Lake City was the fatal stabbing of a Black woman by three white men near Lake City, Williamsburg County, South Carolina, reported in November 1888. She was killed while trying to protect her son, whom the men were beating, and the dispatch reporting the killing said the attackers remained at large with no effort made to arrest them.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jerry Taylor
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jerry Taylor was the killing of a Black man in St. Helena Parish, Louisiana, on the night of November 22, 1888. He was accused of criminally assaulting the thirteen-year-old daughter of J. C. Williams. The case reached the press only as one-sentence wire and digest items, which ran in papers from Washington and New York to Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa and Dakota over the following week.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jim Smith
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jim Smith was the killing of a Black man by a mob of white men in Crittenden County, Arkansas, in late November 1888. Smith, accused of an offense against a white farmer's wife, was taken from a deputy sheriff on the way to jail at Marion and shot. The case reached readers only through brief wire items in papers outside Arkansas.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of Bald Knobber witnesses (1888)
episodes.lead: The reported lynching of Bald Knobber witnesses was a November 1888 telegraph story that five men who had testified against the Bald Knobber leader Dave Walker had been hanged by former members of the band on Bull Creek in Christian County, Missouri. A detailed special from Ozark named the dead and described about 200 disguised riders, but on the same day a messenger from Bull Creek said no one had been lynched. No confirmation followed, and a Springfield resident later called the story "an unmitigated hoax."

episodes.title: Reported lynching of Joe Taylor
episodes.lead: The reported lynching of Joe Taylor was a mob killing said to have taken place in Texas, apparently at Texarkana, in early November 1888, known only from a dispatch received by Taylor's relatives in West Virginia. One version held that Taylor, accused of shooting a man, was about to be lynched, while a Parkersburg wire said a mob had taken him from prison and hanged him. Papers outside Texas carried the story as news of a native West Virginian, and no report from Texas confirming it appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Killing of John Cain
episodes.lead: The killing of John Cain was the fatal shooting of a Black man by a white man, Dave Hancock, at Blackburn, Missouri, on November 6, 1888. According to the only report found, a Sweet Springs correspondence in the Lexington Intelligencer, the trouble grew out of a political discussion and Cain died instantly.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of John Glenn
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of John Glenn took place at Sandy Hill, Washington County, New York, on November 7, 1888, when a crowd tried to seize Glenn, a baseball player accused of assaulting a nine-year-old girl, from the policemen who had arrested him. In the struggle a policeman's revolver went off and the ball struck Glenn in the neck; most reports called the shooting accidental, while one wire brief said a member of the mob fired. A Vermont paper reported a week later that Glenn had died.

episodes.title: Lynching of Judson Cason
episodes.lead: The lynching of Judson Cason was the killing of a Black man, accused of cutting John L. Bryan, who was seized near Lloyd's Station, Jefferson County, Florida, on election day, November 6, 1888, and found dead in the Miccosukie Sinks. A coroner's jury named eight men, among them Bryan, and a grand jury reportedly indicted four while Bryan remained a fugitive. Northern papers took particular notice because Bryan was the son of the writer Mary E. Bryan, who said her son thought he was doing right.

episodes.title: Near-lynching of Lock Johnson in Sweet Springs, Missouri
episodes.lead: The near-lynching of Lock Johnson took place in Sweet Springs, Missouri, in early November 1888, when Johnson, a Black man accused of stabbing a young man of the town, was captured by a posse and "narrowly escaped" lynching. Johnson was not killed, and the episode is known from a single paragraph in the Lexington Intelligencer.

episodes.title: Lynching of Macum Marshall
episodes.lead: The lynching of Macum Marshall was the killing of a Black man by a posse of armed men near Blackshear, Georgia, on November 2, 1888. Marshall was accused of raping Mrs. Henry Howard, a farmer's wife, in her home that morning, and was captured in a nearby swamp and lynched the same day. The story reached readers in Savannah, Kentucky and California as a short wire item.

episodes.title: Corning, Ohio, lynching threat (1888)
episodes.lead: The Corning, Ohio, lynching threat was a threatened lynching in November 1888 of a Black prisoner held for the killing of Pete Donnelly, a railroad brakeman, at Corning. Lee Burrell and Mel Green, both described as "colored," were charged with the murder, and the prisoner was moved to New Lexington before a lynching party could act. The Cleveland Gazette, a Black weekly, reported that the mayor of nearby Rendville had warned Corning's officers that the town's Black residents would retaliate if the man were lynched.

episodes.title: Killing of Mike Tillman
episodes.lead: The killing of Mike Tillman took place on November 29, 1888, Thanksgiving Day, in Yamacraw, a Black quarter of Savannah, Georgia, when Patrolman Pat McMurray shot Tillman, a Black man he had arrested, during a struggle over the officer's club. Tillman died that evening, and the shooting set off a crowd attack in which McMurray, a second patrolman and a white laborer were beaten unconscious. Newspapers across the country reported the episode as a "negro riot", while a coroner's jury found Tillman killed by "party or parties unknown" over the dissent of its three Black members.

episodes.title: Killing of Oscar Carmichael
episodes.lead: The killing of Oscar Carmichael was the shooting of an escaped Georgia convict by a posse at his wife's house in or near Henry County, Georgia, on the night of Friday, November 16, 1888, hours after he was accused of killing his guard, W. J. Gresham, near Griffin. Reports said the posse "riddled" him with shot or bullets, and differed on whether he died in an exchange of fire or was fired on as he approached the house. A Griffin wire story about the guard's death and the bloodhound chase ran in papers from Minnesota to Texas under headlines such as "Speedy Vengeance Overtakes a Prisoner Who Murdered His Guard."

episodes.title: Lynching near Osceola, Arkansas (1888)
episodes.lead: The lynching near Osceola, Arkansas, was the killing in 1888 of an unnamed Black man accused of sexually assaulting a white married woman, as reported by the Osceola Times. It is known only from a one-sentence item in a Missouri weekly of November 24, 1888, which gives no date, place, names or account of the killers.

episodes.title: Pocahontas police shooting and clash of 1888
episodes.lead: The Pocahontas police shooting and clash of 1888 began when a policeman at Pocahontas shot and killed a Black man on the night of Saturday, November 17, 1888, while, by the report, the man was resisting arrest. Three nights later a large crowd of Black residents tried to lynch the policeman, and in the fight that followed one Black man was killed and several were wounded. The only report found, a Lynchburg telegram printed in the Richmond Dispatch, described it as another clash between the races at Pocahontas.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Smith Wallace
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Smith Wallace was reported from Loveland, Ohio, on November 1, 1888: talk of hanging him followed his preliminary hearing on a charge of attempted rape. Wallace was not harmed; he was bound over to the grand jury and lodged in the Clermont County jail at Batavia, and the only report credited "cool heads" with preventing a lynching.

episodes.title: Killing of Stephen Anthony
episodes.lead: The killing of Stephen Anthony was the fatal shooting of a 60-year-old Wallingford, Connecticut, man by his son-in-law, Solon G. Jenkins, at the door of Anthony's home on the evening of 15 November 1888. A wire report carried in western papers said that "angry citizens" threatened to lynch Jenkins after his arrest, though Connecticut papers made no mention of a crowd. Jenkins was bound over for trial and hanged himself in the New Haven County Jail on 20 December 1888.

episodes.title: Lynching of Tim Smith and John Coleman
episodes.lead: The lynching of Tim Smith and John Coleman took place on the night of Tuesday, November 27, 1888, when white men took the two Black men from a convict stockade near Danburg, Wilkes County, Georgia, and, by most accounts, drowned them in the Broad River. The same party whipped two other Black people, Hulda or Huldah Smith and a male relative. Dispatches called it a "race war" arising from a cotton dispute and an alleged insult to a white woman, and the Augusta Chronicle denounced it as "crimes against civilization and Christianity."

episodes.title: Killing of William Durant and lynching of Silas Jeffries and Abe Davis
episodes.lead: The killing of William Durant and lynching of Silas Jeffries and Abe Davis took place near Tushomma, Indian Territory, in November 1888, when a stockman was shot dead outside his home and his friends then hunted down and killed two neighbors suspected of leading his killers. Three men died, and no arrest, inquest or trial appears in the coverage. A single wire dispatch from Little Rock, Arkansas, carried the story to papers from Washington to St. Paul, where headlines called the second killings a "lynching", "retaliation" or the work of "avengers".

episodes.title: Lynching of Wilson Arnold
episodes.lead: The lynching of Wilson Arnold was the killing of a Black man, also named in the papers as Wilkes or Wilks Arnold, who was taken from the jail at Yazoo City, Mississippi, by an armed mob on November 19, 1888, and hanged. Arnold had surrendered to the sheriff about a week earlier after shooting Captain Robert Johnson, a white planter, near Satartia, a killing he said was in self-defense. A Yazoo County grand jury later reported that it could not identify any of the lynchers, although about fifteen were said to be known.

episodes.title: Killing of Adam Golden
episodes.lead: The killing of Adam Golden occurred on a Monday night in December 1888, when a masked mob stoning the house of Jennie Maddox, seven miles north of Buchanan in Haralson County, Georgia, beat and shot to death Golden, a Black man who had intervened. Five white men and two Black men were jailed for the murder and three white women were held for taking part. The story ran on the telegraph across the country, where it appeared beside reports of White Cap outrages and under headlines such as "Killed for His Interference."

episodes.title: McGaheysville dance dynamiting
episodes.lead: The McGaheysville dance dynamiting was an attack on the night of December 26, 1888, in which a dynamite cartridge exploded under a house near McGaheysville, Rockingham County, Virginia, where a party of Black people were holding a dance. The blast nearly destroyed the building and left Amos Moore and two women reported fatally injured. A Harrisonburg dispatch carried in papers across the country reported that threats of lynching followed.

episodes.title: Tackett's Mills riot
episodes.lead: The Tackett's Mills riot was a fight between white and Black men at a country store at Tackett's Mills, Stafford County, Virginia, on Christmas Day 1888. A white man, Bennett (or Benton) Heflin, was shot dead, and a Black man, named Henry Brown in a later report, died of his injuries. Papers across the country reported it as a 'race riot' arising from the recent election, and Fredericksburg feared further trouble.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Emanuel Gaskin
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Emanuel Gaskin took place in Kershaw County, South Carolina, near Camden, in December 1888, when a crowd tried to lynch Gaskin, a Black man accused of murdering a woman named Betsy Clark. Gaskin was hurried away to jail, and one account credits the sheriff and his deputies with rescuing him. Northern papers carried the story chiefly for the alleged murder, reporting the lynching attempt in a closing sentence.

episodes.title: Bross hoodoo story and manhunt
episodes.lead: The Bross hoodoo story was a December 1888 newspaper account from Kingman County, Kansas, that an elderly Black servant had tortured her employer's daughter, whom she believed had 'hoodooed' her, and that a posse was hunting the servant to lynch her. No paper reported her capture, and within days a Kansas paper dismissed the story as a lie.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bud Spears
episodes.lead: The lynching of Bud Spears was the killing of a Black man by a party of masked men who rode up to his house near the Roberts place, twelve miles northwest of Meridian, Mississippi, on Wednesday, December 26, 1888. The attackers acted on a report that Spears was the ringleader of a conspiracy among local Black residents to kill certain white men, a claim the Meridian dispatch traced to an unnamed old man and an overheard conversation. Another Black man at the house was wounded, and in the days that followed white residents arrested Black men as suspected conspirators, seven of whom were acquitted before a justice of the peace. A Times-Democrat special carried the story nationally in January 1889 under headlines that called it a lynching and "Mississippi Race Troubles."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Albert Bulow
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Albert Bulow took place at the Morrison County jail in Little Falls, Minnesota, in early December 1888, when about 150 people came before dawn to seize Bulow, who was charged with murder. Sheriff Rasicot, warned by telegram, had already taken Bulow and a second prisoner, Frank Randall, out of the jail, and the crowd left after searching it. Minnesota and out-of-state papers reported it as a sheriff saving a murderer from a mob.

episodes.title: Lynching of an unnamed gambler near Cumberland Gap, Tennessee
episodes.lead: The lynching of an unnamed gambler near Cumberland Gap, Tennessee, took place in mid-December 1888, when a mob took a Black man from the posse that had arrested him and hanged him from a tree. He was accused of leading an armed party that fired on a railroad contractor's camp after laborers had driven him away. The story ran as a short wire item in papers across the country, and later weekly digests misreported it as the lynching of a man who had fatally wounded a "Captain Dunnavant" near Chattanooga.

episodes.title: Killing of Sam Moore and threatened lynching of Lawson Adams
