episodes.lead: The killing of Sam Moore and threatened lynching of Lawson Adams took place at Gadsden, Alabama, on December 9, 1888, when Moore, described as a Black man accused of a killing, was killed while resisting arrest and Adams, jailed as his supposed accomplice, was expected to be lynched. Wire reports said a mob had gathered at Gadsden and that troops had been asked for, but no report of what became of Adams was found. Papers across the country carried the story in the same days as the Birmingham jail riot, some under headlines that looked ahead to a lynching.

episodes.title: Wahalak race riot
episodes.lead: The Wahalak race riot was an armed clash near Wahalak, Kemper County, Mississippi, on December 16, 1888, in which Black men at the home of a Black man named Maury fired on a white posse, followed by a white manhunt in which Black homes were burned. Between two and five white men were reported killed, among them Constable Seth Cobb and Henry Maury. Three Black captives were later said by their guards to have "escaped," and other Black men were reported shot or hanged, reports that Meridian dispatches denied.

episodes.title: Lynching of George Witherell
episodes.lead: The lynching of George Witherell took place at Canon City, Colorado, early on December 4, 1888, when armed men broke into the jail, shot him and hanged him from a pole. Witherell had been returned to Canon City the day before to stand trial for the murder of a freighter, Charles McCain. The Associated Press account ran nationwide, dwelling on his fight in the cell and the other killings he was accused of.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Henry Briggs
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Henry Briggs took place in Chicago on the morning of December 17, 1888, when a crowd of factory workers and passers-by chased a man accused of attempting to assault a young factory employee, crying "Hang him!" Police intervention saved him, and he was later charged before a justice and let off with a fine.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Herman Luther
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Herman Luther took place in Detroit, Michigan, on December 18, 1888, when a street crowd seized and beat Luther moments after he fired a revolver at his divorced wife and children outside the city hall. Police, and by one account the sheriff and his deputies, took Luther away alive before the crowd could hang him. Papers across the country carried the story by wire, several under headlines such as "Nearly Lynched" and "Luther Deserves Lynching."

episodes.title: Reported White Cap whipping of James McDonald at Agra, Kansas
episodes.lead: The reported White Cap whipping of James McDonald took place, according to a correspondent of the Kansas City Times, at Agra, Kansas, on the night of Monday, December 10, 1888, when a masked band calling itself the "Kansas Division of White Caps" tied him to a telegraph pole and flogged him. Later dispatches said McDonald died of his injuries, and newspapers across the country ran the story as a White Cap murder. Phillips County officials and Kansas papers denounced the whole report as a fabrication, and no independent confirmation of the whipping or the death appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Jed Pritteheft
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Jed Pritteheft was a reported plan by a large crowd of citizens of 'Pittsburgh county' to lynch Pritteheft, a Black man accused of assaulting an eight-year-old girl, around December 26, 1888. No attack on him was reported; he was taken to jail at Lynchburg, Virginia, and the episode survives only as one paragraph in the Richmond Dispatch.

episodes.title: Killing of Howell and pursuit of Jim Newton
episodes.lead: The killing of Howell and pursuit of Jim Newton took place in December 1888 in Stevens County, Kansas, when a farmer named Howell was reported beaten and shot to death by Jim Newton, described as a notorious horse thief, and a posse of farmers set out after Newton. Several versions of the wire story said the posse meant to lynch Newton, but no report of his capture appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Butte anti-Chinese lynching threats, 1888
episodes.lead: The Butte anti-Chinese lynching threats of December 1888 were crowd threats against Chinese residents of Butte, Montana Territory, after a white miner, John Braden, died of a saw wound from a Chinese woodcutter. One dispatch said a crowd chased a Chinese man to hang him, but local reports described only threats, and no one was harmed. A Chinese man arrested as the suspect was held about a week before witnesses testified he was the wrong man.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Lawson Adams
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Lawson Adams occurred at Gadsden, Alabama, in December 1888, when a mob was reported threatening to lynch Adams, who had been jailed as a supposed accomplice of Sam Moore, a Black man accused of killing a man. A Chattanooga Times dispatch of December 9 predicted that Adams would be lynched before morning, and the story ran in papers from Georgia to California under headlines such as "Lynching Looked For" and "More Lynching in Prospect." The coverage does not report what became of Adams.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of E. J. Wright
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of E. J. Wright took place at Pocatello, Idaho, on December 22, 1888, when a mob of railroad switchmen and brakemen surrounded the depot where officers held Wright after he shot a brakeman, L. F. Durfee. Wright was first reported dying of a neck wound, but a week later he was recovering in the Blackfoot jail after a coroner's jury exonerated him.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Milt Parker
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Milt Parker was a reported threat against a Black man accused of assaulting a white girl near Bantam, Ohio, in late December 1888. A brief telegraphic dispatch said he would be lynched when caught, but the coverage reports no capture, attack or killing.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of a street dentist's patient in New Orleans
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of a street dentist's patient in New Orleans was a mob attack on an unnamed Black man that took place on or before December 1888, after a rumor spread that he was killing a white boy. Police stopped the mob before he was beaten to death, and the case reached the northern press as an ironic example of how 'the race issue' filled southern papers.

episodes.title: Lynching of Noah Taylor
episodes.lead: The lynching of Noah Taylor was the hanging of a Black man by a body of men who took him from the jail at Harrisonburg, Catahoula Parish, Louisiana, in December 1888. Taylor had been arrested as a suspect in the ambush killing of R. N. Stegall on a road below Harrisonburg a few days earlier. A Times-Democrat dispatch from Natchez carried the story to papers across the country, some of which set it against the news from Birmingham, Alabama, where a sheriff had defended his jail against a mob.

episodes.title: Barnwell County race-war scare (1888)
episodes.lead: The Barnwell County race-war scare was an armed mobilization of white residents near Bamberg, South Carolina, in December 1888, who searched the swamps for Black men supposed to have kidnapped and murdered a white farmer, Robert Morris. Morris was found alive and drunk in the woods two days after he disappeared, and no one of either race was reported harmed. Papers across the country first carried the episode as a threatened "war of races" and then retold its ending as a joke.

episodes.title: Regulator attack on the Witherspoon house, York County, South Carolina
episodes.lead: The Regulator attack on the Witherspoon house was a night assault on the home of Dave Witherspoon, a Black man, in York County, South Carolina, on Sunday, December 23, 1888. Witherspoon fired from inside and killed William J. Harten, a white attacker, and a coroner's jury found he had acted in self-defense. A Charlotte wire dispatch instead named the Black man 'Sam Harting' and said he would be lynched if caught.

episodes.title: Killing of Sam Moore
episodes.lead: The killing of Sam Moore took place near Gadsden, Alabama, on December 9, 1888, when deputy sheriffs searching for Moore, a Black man accused of killing a man the night before, found and killed him. The deputies had been shot and wounded by unknown attackers during the search, and they jailed a second man, Lawson Adams, as Moore's supposed accomplice. Papers across the country carried the story chiefly as a forecast that Adams would be lynched.

episodes.title: Lynching of Van Canady
episodes.lead: The lynching of Van Canady was the hanging of a young Black man, also called John Carson, by a crowd that took him from the jail at Shelby, North Carolina, just after midnight on December 1-2, 1888. Canady had been accused of murdering James Philbeck, a white farmer, and was reported to have confessed the day before. A coroner's jury found that he died "at the hands of parties unknown", and the story ran as a brief across the country, while North Carolina papers called the lynching just punishment.

episodes.title: Lynching of W. D. French
episodes.lead: The lynching of W. D. French took place in Greeley, Colorado, on the night of December 28-29, 1888, when a body of masked men broke into the county jail, took out French and hanged him to a tree. French, a cattle owner and farmer, was being held with three other men for the killing of Harry Woodbury at Evans about two weeks earlier. No member of the mob was identified, and most papers reported the lynching only as a short wire item.

episodes.title: Westport hanging of two men (1888)
episodes.lead: The Westport hanging of two men was the discovery, reported on the evening of December 12, 1888, of the bodies of two unidentified men hanging from a tree near a school house south of Westport, in Jackson County, Missouri. Newspapers supposed the men were horse thieves lynched by farmers, vigilantes or an anti-horse-thief association, but no report named the dead or the men who hanged them. The item ran as a brief in papers from Minnesota and Kansas to California, Wisconsin, Dakota and Rhode Island over the following ten days.

episodes.title: Lynching of three Black people in York County, South Carolina
episodes.lead: The lynching of three Black people in York County, South Carolina, is known from a single passing reference in a December 1888 dispatch, which recalled that a grand jury had been asked to look into "the lynching of three negroes in that county." The dispatch cited the case because the presiding judge, Judge Pressley, had told the grand jury that investigation was almost useless, as no jury would be likely to convict.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Frank B. Mason
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Frank B. Mason took place in West Virginia some time before November 1888, when a mob took Mason, a theft suspect, out of a jail and hanged him three times to make him confess. Mason survived, and his account reached readers through an Ohio State Journal interview that papers in three states reprinted.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Jack Raymond ("No Longer a Mystery" story)
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Jack Raymond is an episode in "No Longer a Mystery," a frontier romance credited to the Chicago Herald and reprinted in American newspapers in the autumn of 1888, in which a mob led by the sheriff took Raymond from the jail at San Felipe in the San Joaquin valley to hang him. In the story the noose was already on his neck when the sheriff's own daughter cut him loose and rode off with him. The piece gives no date for the mob and presents itself as a legend told by pioneer settlers, not as a news report.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of Mark Dorlon
episodes.lead: The reported lynching of Mark Dorlon was a killing of a Brooklyn youth in Arizona in 1888, known only from the account of a companion, Robert Eaton, who returned to Brooklyn that December. Eaton said Dorlon had been lynched for horse-stealing by "Cowboys," but he had only heard the news secondhand, and no date, place or confirmation appeared in the coverage.

episodes.title: Reported lynching of Michael Dohm
episodes.lead: The reported lynching of Michael Dohm was an unconfirmed account, published in Wahpeton, Dakota Territory, in June 1888, that a local man had been lynched in Texas for horse stealing. The story rested on a letter his wife was said to have received, which the Wahpeton paper never saw and which men who knew him doubted.

episodes.title: Lynching of Mosier (Cheyenne, Wyoming Territory)
episodes.lead: The lynching of Mosier was the hanging of a man accused of murder by a mob that broke open the jail at Cheyenne, Wyoming Territory, sometime before 1888. According to a later account, seventy-five men took him from the jail on a Sunday night and hanged him from a telegraph pole before about 2,000 people, despite pleas from the Secretary of the Territory and the mayor. The Cheyenne Leader still cited the case in 1888 as a local precedent, and a railroad story reprinted that year called it "one of the most famous lynchings ever known in the far West."

episodes.title: Lynching of John Ninna and Slume
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Ninna and Slume was the hanging of two Kootenai men by a party of white settlers north of Flathead Lake in Missoula county, Montana, in March 1888, at a place a settler's letter called Penny's mill. The settlers accused them of joining in the killing of three white prospectors on Wolf Creek the previous summer; a third accused man escaped. The hanging set off a brief settler alarm and a petition for troops, but no hostilities were reported and later accounts called the scare exaggerated.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of two tramps at Rock Springs
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of two tramps at Rock Springs was a mob hanging in Wyoming Territory, reported in July 1888, in which residents strung up two unnamed men suspected of a robbery. Both men protested their innocence and were let down alive just before death, after which they left town. Wyoming papers repeated the story in brief as a warning to tramps.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of William Springer
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of William Springer was talk among citizens of Colton and San Bernardino, California, of lynching Springer after he was accused of murdering his bride in a Colton hotel around the turn of 1887. Springer was never found alive, and nearly two years later hunters found his skeleton north of San Bernardino with a revolver and a bullet hole in the head. The lynch talk is known only from a San Francisco Call retrospective reprinted when his remains were found in November 1888.
